entries.summary: <p>Riot Fest got off to a late, muddy and soggy start on Sunday, the last day of the annual music festival in Douglass Park. </p><p>Largemouth and Sincere Engineer represented Chicago punk rock to kick off the day. entries.title: Sox knock off Tigers to keep pace with Guardians
entries.summary: <p>Davis Martin is still looking for his 10<sup>th</sup> win, but he pitched well enough on Sunday to set the stage for a more critical White Sox victory.</p><p>Martin tossed scoreless ball for 4 1/3 innings, then the bullpen took over as the White Sox cruised past the Detroit Tigers 8-1 to remain one game behind division-leading Cleveland in the American League Central. </p><p>Chase Meidroth smacked his 15<sup>th</sup> homer, a two run-shot in the fifth to open a 6-0 lead, after Sam Antonacci laced a two-run double in the South Siders’ three-run fourth. Kyle Teel, Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Randal Grichuk also came through with RBIs as the Sox took three of four from the Tigers and improved to 80-76.</p><p>The Sox put it away with two runs in the eighth, completing a 10-hit attack.</p><p>The game was scheduled to start at 1:10 p.m.,but the first pitch was delayed by persistent light rain to 5 p.m. The Sox already knew the Guardians had edged the Athletics 1-0 for a fifth straight win by then.</p><p>Martin entered Sunday off three effective outings since returning from the injured list from a right middle finger blister on Sept 2. He came through with a fourth against Detroit The right-hander allowed three hits, walking two, hitting a batter and striking out six before exiting after 70 pitches (43 for strikes).</p><p>Hagen Smith, Huascar Brazobán, Trevor Richards and Luis Castillo followed. Only Richards, who tossed the seventh and eight innings, was touched for a run. Brazobán (6-2) tossed a scoreless sixth inning for the win.</p><p>Martin still isn’t as dominant as earlier this season, when he raced a 9-2 record. He earned that ninth win on June 10 by tossing six shutout innings against Atlanta.</p><p>That’s the last time he got a “W.” It was 99 days ago. Martin is still 9-7 overall, but he lowered his ERA to 3.84 on Sunday.</p><p>And since returning from his blister, Martin has given the White Sox rotation some desperately needed stability. </p><p>Although the right-hander is 0-1 with three no-decisions, Martin has allowed just three runs (two earned) in 20 1/3 innings in three starts and a bulk relief appearance in Cleveland last Tuesday. That works out to a 0.89 ERA. He’s allowed 16 hits, walked six and struck out 10.</p><p>Martin dodged a bullet in the top of the second Sunday when Brett Callahan flew out to Brenton Doyle at the right-center wall for the third out.</p><p>The White Sox took a 1-0 lead in the bottom half when Meidroth stole second and scored on Montgomery’s double down the right-field line.</p><p>Martin allowed a single and walk with two outs in the fourth, but struck out Spencer Torkelson to end the threat. </p><p>The Sox extended the lead to 4-0 in the fourth, scoring on Antonacci’s double and Teel’s single with two outs</p><p>Antonacci made it 3-0 when he laced Troy Melton’s low slider down the right field line to drive in two runs. The previous hitter, Brenton Doyle, had kept the inning alive by beating out a chopper to third for an infield single. Then Teel bounced an RBIs single through the right side</p><p>Meidroth hit his two-run shot to the left field bullpen off Ty Madden gave the Sox some breathing room.</p><p><b>ABS Forced Turning Point</b></p><p>Smith relieved Martin with a runner on first and one out in the fifth and the Sox ahead 4-0. Smith walked two to load the bases, but escaped by striking out Hao-Yu Lee and getting Riley Greene to ground out to first.</p><p>But there was a twist</p><p>With runners on first and second and one out in the fifth, Detroit’s Gleyber Torres successfully used the ABS challenges on two consecutive called strikes. Both were overturned to balls and he walked to load the bases.</p><p><b>Peters Still Sore</b></p><p>White Sox outfielder Tristan Peters remained out of the lineup on Sunday after hitting the right-center wall hard trying to snare Kevin McGonigle’s bases-clearing triple on Friday. Brenton Doyle played in center field and Braden Montgomery in right.</p><p>Peters smashed his shoulder and fell to the warning track before exiting Friday. But he pinch-ran for Tommy Pham in the eighth Sunday and scored.</p><p>Manager Will Venable didn’t rule out a full return for Peters on Tuesday in Kansas City.</p>

entries.title: Munetaka Murakami working hard to emerge from slump
entries.summary: <p>Slumping slugger <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> has three hits in his last four games, including a three-run home run (No. 32) and his first triple in the majors. Still, the big rookie from Japan is batting only .108 (8-for-74) over his last 22 games, with three homers, 12 RBI and 15 walks.</p><p>Murakami says he expected major-league pitchers to quickly analyze him after he got off to a strong start this season that included 20 homers in his first 57 games — and before he suffered a hamstring strain May 29 that sent him to the injured list for six weeks.</p><p>“I’m not surprised by the adjustment the pitchers have been doing,” Murakami said after homering Thursday to power a 3-1 series-opening win over the Tigers. “Obviously, if you get at-bats here at the major-league level, they’re going to be looking at my weak points and weaknesses along with the at-bats.</p><p>“It’s just to overcome those every time, and I have to keep continuing that so I can be better.”</p><p>Before the rain-delayed series finale Sunday, an 8-1 victory over Detroit, manager <b>Will Venable </b>said Murakami has been working on some changes.</p><p>“He’s made some mechanical adjustments with his setup that have put him in a better spot to make more contact,” Venable said. “He’s probably, after making more contact and hitting the ball hard, feeling more confident and feeling good about himself.”</p><p>Murakami insists he doesn’t doubt himself.</p><p>“It doesn’t matter how I swing at the ball and what my mechanics are at the moment,” he said. “It’s just about getting that win every day. Winning is all that matters at the moment right now.”</p><p><b>Bears blasphemy</b></p><p><b>Miguel Vargas</b> was clapping his hands over his head and performing his rendition of the “Skol Chant” — a pregame ritual for Vikings fans — from his corner locker in the clubhouse before the game.</p><p>Vargas, 26, became the first player in franchise history with at least 30 home runs, 30 doubles, 20 stolen bases and 100 runs scored in a season in the Sox’ 3-1 victory Saturday. He went deep for the 33rd time, walked twice, scored twice, stole a base and made a diving stop on <b>Dillon Dingler’s</b> sharp grounder to third.</p><p>So teammates might have been willing to cut Vargas, a big Vikings fan, a little slack.</p><p>Vargas started to follow the Vikings thanks to his friendship with Cubs first baseman <b>Michael Busch</b>, a native of the Twin Cities suburb of Inner Grove Heights, Minnesota. The two were teammates and roommates in the Dodgers’ organization.</p><p>Vargas and a handful of teammates visited the Vikings’ training facility last September, when the Sox swept a four-game series against the Twins in Minneapolis.</p><p><b>Fresh arm for the bullpen</b></p><p>If nothing else, the Sox gained a fresh bullpen arm when they reinstated right-hander <b>Huascar Brazoban</b> from the injured list.</p><p>They optioned left-hander <b>Chris Murphy</b> to Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>Brazoban, 36, acquired from the Mets at the trade deadline for two minor-league pitchers, had been out since Aug. 25 because of a left lat strain, then a rehab stint with the Knights.</p><p>He has pitched 10 innings in 10 appearances with the Sox and was 0-0 with a 6.30 ERA.</p><p>With Charlotte, Brazoban was 0-1 with a 3.38 ERA in 5„ innings over five games.</p><p>“Braz is in a good spot,’’ Venable said. “Got him back and healthy and feeling good.”</p><p>Brazoban has been charged with at least one run in six of his 10 outings (seven runs total) with the South Siders, allowing two homers, 12 hits and six walks.</p><p>He was better with the Mets in 46 games and 52„ innings before the trade, going 5-2 with a 2.56 ERA.</p><p>Murphy is 3-0 with a 4.81 ERA and one save in 33 appearances this season in several stints with the Sox.</p>

entries.title: Riot Fest Day 3 gets off to late and soggy start; William Shatner and Patti Smith perform
entries.summary: <p>After heavy rains pummeled the Chicago area overnight and Sunday, organizers delayed the start of Riot Fest by a few hours as crews tried to clean up the grounds at Douglass Park.</p><p>But with continued rain throughout the day, the park grew muddier and muddier, making it difficult for festgoers to navigate from stage to stage. People were seen getting stuck in the mud, and shoes were left behind in the sludge.</p><p>Mother and daughter Sue and Shannon Staszak came to the festival to see Patti Smith and Elvis Costello.</p><p>“I don’t care about rain, but this is epic mud,” Sue said, adding, “I worry for other people when I see them slip. It’s the mother in me.”</p><p>The weather prompted the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/20/rain-thunderstorms-flooding-chicago-river-swim-weather" target="_blank" >cancellation of other events in the area Sunday</a>, including the Chicago River Swim, but Riot Fest pressed on with the final day. Sunday’s anticipated acts included the debut of 95-year-old William Shatner and his metal band The *uckers, ’90s icon Alanis Morissette and Chicago-born Patti Smith. </p><p>Read on for reviews of some of Sunday’s standout sets.</p><h3>William Shatner</h3><p>At 95 years old, “Star Trek” legend William Shatner has explored his latest new frontier — fronting a metal band at a music festival.</p><p>The actor/commercial guru debuted the project at Riot Fest Sunday, giving some fans a sneak peek at a sanctioned aftershow at Park West Saturday night. And it was everything fans could’ve hoped for — a mix of dramatic flair, his nonsensical banter and some solid music curation.</p><p>He was backed by The *Uckers, a hair metal motley crew featuring guitarist and musical director Marcus Nand (also of Mike Tramp, Candice Night), bassist Phil Soussan (Ozzy Osbourne, Billy Idol), guitarist Britt Lightning (Vixen, Cactus) and drummer Fred Aching (Kings of Thrash, Dead Groove, Fraxures).</p><p>The set offered ubiquitous metal covers of classics like Ozzy Osbourne’s “Crazy Train.” Shatner didn’t sing as much as he delivered spoken word diatribes that drew on his theater background. It’s also not far off from what he’s done musically in the past.</p><p>Shatner’s performance on Sunday sent a positive message — you can always find ways to “live long and prosper” and achieve your wildest dreams no matter your age.</p><h3>Patti Smith</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“I was born in a blizzard in Chicago, so I guess I’m a bad weather girl,” Patti Smith said at the top of her set, trying to give the crowd any kind of explanation for Sunday’s unstoppable rain that turned Douglass Park into a shell of itself by the evening performance.</p><p>It was difficult to find any patch of grass to stand on within the growing mud explosion. Attendees were seen getting stuck in pits trying to make their way to the Rise Stage, though making it felt like a victory to take in the glory of the punk poet.</p><p>Unsurprisingly she had one of the most political sets of the weekend, opening strongly with “People Have the Power.”</p><p>“In 1986, Fred ‘Sonic’ Smith and I wrote this song for the future and the future is now,” she said to introduce the anthemic classic. “Chicago, don’t forget it, use your voice!”</p><p> Later, Smith dedicated “Pissing in a River” to the beleaguered Lake Ontario and also took a few moments to discuss Palestinians ahead of a reverent “Peaceable Kingdom.”</p><p>“Twenty-three years ago we wrote this song for the Palestinian people. That was 23 years ago and we had at that time some hope that the world would ban together and people would do the right thing,” she said, calling the conflict “one of the great heartbreaks of our time,” adding, “We will always hope for the Palestinian people and this song is for them.” </p><p>The hourlong set was a masterful display of Smith’s powerful messages and creative songwriting. Smith and Her Band, including the venerable Lenny Kaye, who just celebrated his new solo album with a show at Metro Friday night, also added in a fired-up “Gloria,” “Break It Up” written with late Television front man Tom Verlaine (and dedicated to Jim Morrison) and the eloquent “Dancing Barefoot” (dedicated to “the girls”). There was even an apropos cover of The Who’s “My Generation” that summed up the feelings of Riot Fest weekend and the cross-generational slew of bands, but also its dissident foundation.</p><p>“My generation had dreams man. We did the best we could but we also brought you know who in the Oval Office,” Smith lamented. “He’s the same age as me, can you believe that s---?!” </p><p>But it was the beloved track “Because the Night” that brought Smith and her platform full circle. “In these times we must make our numbers grow and stick together,” she said ahead of the song, “so we can somehow make a better f------ world.”</p><h3>Sincere Engineer</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6d0000" Rezin/Sun-Times</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Chicago music continued to have a strong presence at Riot Fest as Sincere Engineer took the stage Sunday afternoon. It marked the fourth time the homegrown punk band has played the event, with previous outings in 2019, 2022 and 2024.</p><p>Like clockwork, the four-piece’s latest appearance was all about corn dogs. Since releasing the 2017 song "Corn Dog Sonnet No. 7,” the foodstuff has become a de facto mascot for the band. Most of the time, there’s at least one person who comes dressed up in a meat-and-bun costume (sans ketchup, where possible) and fans routinely engage in a corn dog mosh pit while holding the carnival food or associated signage.</p><p>But this year took the obsession to a whole new level, as DoorDash crew members handed out free corn dogs just as Sincere Engineer launched into the song.</p><p>“I’ve also never played in a raincoat or boots before,” singer Deanna Belos added about another new milestone for the band, driven by the day’s abysmal weather.</p><p>“This feels strange. It looks like we are all at the Bass Pro Shop. … Do I look like Oasis in this jacket?” she joked, referencing the outerwear favored by the British band’s singer Liam Gallagher.</p><p>Belos’ candor and fun-natured attitude is just one of the attributes that have drawn fans to Sincere Engineer’s orbit over the past 10 years the band has been active. In 2025, the group released its anniversary documentary, “Nobody’s Gonna Do It for You,” which covered its consistent rise as part of Chicago’s new punk wave.</p><p>Hard-edged songs like “Twist My Tongue” and “Anemia” have also put Sincere Engineer on the map. They wisely added both to the set along with cuts from 2026 album “Probable Claws,” which continues to give them a strong grip. of Riot Fest, shortly after the rain delay lifted and gates opened at 2 p.m.</p><p>“If you’re scared, you should’ve stayed the f--- home!” screamed 16-year-old singer Jorgie Santopoalo to start the set. There was no fear to be found on the faces of the few dozen who raced from the main entrance to catch the set, dodging pools of water and mud pits along the way.</p><p>Along with his brothers, 15-year-old bassist Jeremy and 11-year-old drummer Oliver, Largemouth is the youngest band to play Riot Fest this year. Especially if you add in the small baby their dad/manager Isaiah brought out at one point, making the kid’s hands clap into the microphone.</p><p>The group, rounded out by 16-year-old percussionist Oliver Mendoza and 18-year-old Diangelo Esquivel, was one of the four community bands booked by Riot Fest to represent talent from the event’s backyard in North Lawndale and Little Village. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/08/17/photos-chicago-held-a-contest-for-stage-time-at-riot-fest-this-teen-punk-rock-band-won" target="_blank" ><u>Largemouth won the final spot</u></a> in a battle of the bands contest during a 24th Ward end-of-summer celebration held in early August. Members are from a little bit of everywhere, however, including the northwest suburbs.</p><p>Their musical blend offers a wide range, too, with Nirvana, Motorhead and a bit of hardcore bubbling up on songs like “Keep a Secret.” On others, the five-piece introduced a jazzy mix and more traditional Latin sounds, furthered by the addition of Mendoza on congas. All of it got the small but mighty crowd moshing and covered in mud, marking another big moment for the young band.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sofie Hernandez-Simeonidis</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/19/photos-aim-high-angine-de-poitrine-morrissey-and-tool-on-riot-fest-day-2" >Photos: Aim High, Angine de Poitrine, Social Distortion, Morrissey and Tool on Riot Fest Day 2</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/19/riot-fest-day-2-chicago-douglass-park" >Riot Fest Day 2 cut short due to weather with ‘torrential downpours’ in the forecast; Tool, Nas and Morrissey sets moved up</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/18/riot-fest-2026-violet-grohl-twenty-one-pilots-rise-against-weather-douglass-park-chicago-music" >Riot Fest 2026 kicks off with rising stars Violet Grohl, the Paradox and return of local punks Rise Against</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs manager Craig Counsell: 'We’ve got to find out about our bullpen' in final week
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — The Cubs will have a lot going on this week, the final one of the regular season. Most important is their pursuit of home-field advantage for a National League wild-card series, which is very much unsettled.</p><p>Not far behind is putting together their bullpen for the playoffs. That was on manager Craig Counsell’s mind after Cubs relievers pitched four scoreless innings to seal a 5-2 victory Saturday against the Reds.</p><p>‘‘I really believe, through this last week of the season, we’ve got to find out about our bullpen,’’ Counsell said after the game. ‘‘We’ve got to find out about guys down there. And this was a good step in that direction.’’</p><p>In fact, Counsell has been thinking about the Cubs’ potential postseason pitching staff for more than a week. The series against the Reds ended a stretch of three series Counsell treated as playoff series, with the help of two days off.</p><p>‘‘I told the relievers that going into this; the starters, the same thing,’’ Counsell said Sunday. ‘‘We’re going to use them like we would use them in a playoff situation. I’ve had guys up more if they haven’t been in a game. You can afford to do that when you get to this point in the year.’’</p><p>Daniel Palencia figures to be a crucial piece to that puzzle after his dominant outing Saturday, when he threw two perfect innings and struck out three, reaching 100 mph several times. After battling through oblique and elbow injuries, Palencia said he feels like himself again.</p><p>‘‘I feel great; I’ve been feeling a lot of confidence,’’ Palencia said. ‘‘I wasn’t trying to throw hard, and when I saw the [velocity], I was like, ‘OK, I’m feeling good.’ ’’</p><p>Palencia pitched the sixth and seventh innings, which is in line with where he pitched last season in the playoffs, despite earning 22 saves during the regular season. He mostly pitched in the fifth and sixth in the postseason and performed well.</p><p>‘‘I’m ready for anything,’’ he said. ‘‘I don’t care if it’s the ninth inning or the fifth; I just want to help the team.’’</p><p>Ryan Zeferjahn knew exactly how he would be used Saturday. He entered with two outs in the eighth to face Reds star Sal Stewart, whom he struck out. Although he retired two batters in the ninth, the last out went to left-hander Ryan Rolison.</p><p>‘‘That’s how we’ve treated these last three series,’’ Zeferjahn said. ‘‘It’s like you get that one-out save or you have pockets. We don’t have roles. When your pocket comes up, you’re ready to go, and it’s all game.’’</p><p>‘‘Knowing how we’re going to use guys is important,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘We went through a stretch where we had some guys struggling, so some things have changed in who we were using and when we were using them. And getting those guys out there as much as we can this last week to get them on track is something that we’re going to try to do.’’</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Cubs one win from second straight playoff berth — common for some, rare for them
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — The Cubs are one victory away from back-to-back playoff berths, a common occurrence for some franchises but an infrequent achievement for a 150-year-old franchise with three World Series titles.</p><p>All they need to do is win Tuesday, when they return to Wrigley Field to face the Marlins, a ballclub that, like several others, has ruined celebration plans before. Fans of certain ages will recall the 1969 Mets, 1984 Padres and 2003 Marlins as teams that brought heartbreak to the North Side.</p><p>The 2016 World Series brought joy to Wrigleyville, but it was expected to bring more — as in more Series titles. That era did bring four consecutive playoff berths, including three trips in a row to the National League Championship Series. It marked only the third set of consecutive postseason appearances in franchise history.</p><p>A fourth set is all but clinched, but it could have happened Sunday. The Cubs entered the day needing a victory against the Reds and a Diamondbacks loss to the Yankees to clinch a wild-card berth. If they won, the Cubs planned to stay in the visitors’ clubhouse at Great American Ball Park and watch the D-backs, whose game started just as the Cubs’ ended.</p><p>The Cubs held up their end, winning 9-1. David Peterson allowed one run in six innings, and Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run and stole his 38th base. But they changed their plans, perhaps in light of Alex Bregman’s injury. The Cubs sent Bregman to the hospital after a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch bloodied his face.</p><p>The D-backs ended up winning, so the Cubs’ departure was for the best. It would have been quite a waste of time to sit in the visitors’ clubhouse — which still had damp carpeting and reeked of beer and champagne from the Dodgers’ celebration of their 13th NL West crown in 14 years — for another few hours.</p><p>The Cubs won’t need anyone’s help Tuesday, though that might come in handy the rest of the week as they try to secure home-field advantage in the wild-card round. With six games left, the Cubs are tied with the Padres for the first wild-card spot but hold the tiebreaker. The Phillies are third, and the Cubs own that tiebreaker, as well.</p><p>But this Cubs team wasn’t put together — and manager Craig Counsell wasn’t brought in — to win wild-card berths. For the third consecutive season, the Cubs will finish in second place in the Central behind the Brewers, from whom they lured Counsell to work his small-market magic at the big-market level.</p><p>It hasn’t gone according to plan because the guy who was Counsell’s bench coach with the Brewers, Pat Murphy, might be getting more out of that club than Counsell did — at least during the regular season. Of course, neither has gotten past the NLCS. But until Counsell and the Cubs pass the Brewers, Murphy’s specter will hover over them.</p><p>Maybe having the best player in baseball will make the difference this season. Crow-Armstrong is likely to be the NL MVP, and the Cubs will need him to play like one in the playoffs. He didn’t last season, batting .185 with no homers and one stolen base in eight games. He even got caught stealing once.</p><p>The fact that he went 0-for-10 in the first two games of the weekend series against the Reds in a hitter-friendly venue was astonishing. He snapped that ‘‘skid’’ Sunday by going 3-for-5 with three runs scored, a double, a homer and two RBI.</p><p>‘‘Every player is begging for a two-game slump,’’ Counsell said. ‘‘You may get him a day or two, but it’s coming.’’</p><p>And with one more victory, the Cubs are coming, too, and they say they’re coming for everything. But they will need everything to click, from their major-league-best offense and defense to their still-undecided pitching staff.</p><p>It’s a different game in the postseason, which this franchise knows all too well — just not often enough from its own experience.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks' power play has new look with Patrick Kane on left, Roman Kantserov as bumper
entries.summary: <p>Most talented forwards arrive in the NHL having played only on the flanks of power-play formations for their junior or college teams because most were stars on those teams.</p><p>That’s not the case, however, for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks?_gl=1*1fn2n99*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTcwMTQyOTU5NC4xNzg5OTQxODgz*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODk5NDE4ODIkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODk5NDE4ODIkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> rookie Roman Kantserov. In Russia, he played not on the flanks but in the bumper role — stationed in the middle of the offensive zone — for Magnitogorsk of the Kontinental Hockey League.</p><p>So Kantserov is uniquely qualified to slide right in as the bumper on the Hawks’ power play, which enters this season manned almost entirely by new personnel after limping to a 29th-place finish last season.</p><p>Kantserov’s previous bumper experience is valuable because it’s not an easy position to learn. Coach Jeff Blashill pointed out it often requires slight movements around the slot for the bumper to open himself up to receive passes, make passes or shoot. It also requires keen awareness to know when to push toward the boards to support teammates in puck battles.</p><p>It might not be a completely seamless <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/29/blackhawks-roman-kantserov-nhl-preparation-english-spencer-knight" target="_blank" >transition for Kantserov</a>, however. He already has realized NHL penalty-killers are better than KHL penalty-killers.</p><p>‘‘In [the] KHL, I was best in this spot on bumper, but now it’s absolutely different,’’ Kantserov said. ‘‘Guys here think faster and bring pressure, and I need to also be stronger, faster, smarter and feel guys.</p><p>‘‘Sometimes I do [a] no-look pass, and I need to know, ‘Where is my mate?’ A couple of games in the season, we [will] understand together.’’</p><p>Surrounding Kantserov on the Hawks’ new-look top unit are Bowen Byram at the point, Patrick Kane on the left flank, Anton Frondell on the right flank and Tyler Bertuzzi down low.</p><p>Connor Bedard’s return from injury eventually will knock somebody (most likely Frondell) down to the second unit, but the Hawks can figure that out later.</p><p>Interestingly, all five of those guys are left-handed. Frondell, whose powerful one-timer was already well-known before he got to the NHL, is set up in the prime one-timer spot.</p><p>That’s because Kane, who has spent most of his career playing on the right flank of power plays, has moved over to the left.</p><p>‘‘I just think this offers him more options in terms of passing,’’ Blashill said. ‘‘It fits our hands better, but it also maybe can fit his skill set.’’</p><p>Kane is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/17/blackhawks-patrick-kane-right-decision" target="_blank" >embracing</a> the challenge. On older Hawks teams, it made sense for right-handed forwards such as Artemi Panarin, Alex DeBrincat and Patrick Sharp to set up on the left for one-timers. Kane recognizes that’s not the case here.</p><p>‘‘If that’s how it’s going to be all year, great; I’ll try to own that spot as much as possible,’’ Kane said. ‘‘When Connor comes back, we [will] switch sides maybe or maybe we stay with that. Who knows? I think it’s nice to have both options if things get a little bit stale.</p><p>‘‘I’ve always felt maybe [by] coming down the left, I could shoot and score a little bit more because the puck is not to the middle of the ice. You can protect it a little bit more. You can shoot and use the screens.’’</p><p>Kane and Kantserov already seem to share a natural connection in the Kane-Panarin mold. They made several pretty plays during a scrimmage Sunday.</p><p>Byram, meanwhile, will get an opportunity to show what he can do as a power-play quarterback. Stuck behind Rasmus Dahlin the last three seasons with the Sabres, he got only scraps on the second unit.</p><p>With the Hawks, Byram is the clear No. 1, leaving Sam Rinzel and Artyom Levshunov — both of whom struggled with quarterbacking last season — to compete for second-unit opportunities. It’s worth noting Rinzel has looked improved in that role during camp.</p><p>‘‘[I’m] trying to work on my movement on the blue line and deception,’’ Byram said.</p>

Dear Abby: Teacher Suspects Parents' Phone Habits Affect Kids
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> You sometimes ask readers to share their pet peeves. I am a public school teacher, and here is mine: Parents wonder why their children misbehave, argue with them and act out with attention-getting behaviors. My advice to them: Put down those cellphones and pay attention to your kids!</p><p>I just had a conference with a mother whose children argue, pout and scream when they are told to do something at home. These children have no special needs and don't demonstrate those behaviors at school. Abby, the woman texted on her phone throughout the meeting. That behavior is not OK.</p><p>The next time I encounter a parent who does it, I will ask the person if he or she would like to suspend the conference to take care of the pressing business. Perhaps these parents need to be embarrassed a bit so they will realize how inappropriate texting or talking on the phone is when face-to-face with another person. — <i>A VENTING EDUCATOR</i></p><p><b>DEAR EDUCATOR:</b> I agree that what the parent did was extremely rude. It sent the unmistakable message that not only was the meeting not important to her, but neither was anything you had to say. If you are asking me for permission to inform parents that cellphones must be silenced and out of sight during conferences with you, you have it. My advice is to say it as soon as the parent enters your classroom. You can frame it as parents following the same rules as students in your space.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have three grown children. One son, "Charles," with his wife and three elementary-school-aged children, rents the house next door to me for about $1,200 a month less than I might charge a nonfamily renter. My other two kids live hundreds of miles away. My younger son, "James," is unmarried and without children. He thinks I'm being unfair to him and his sister because I'm not charging the maximum rent the house might get, thereby reducing his inheritance. I place great value in having Charles and his family living next door to me. James thinks I should be regularly compensating him and his sister for what he claims I'm giving to Charles and his family. What do you think? — <i>LANDLORD DAD</i></p><p><b>DEAR LANDLORD DAD:</b> I think it's presumptuous and ill-mannered of your younger son to count his inheritance while his father is still living and breathing. Charles' rent is between you and him, and frankly, James shouldn't be privy to the details of the arrangement. Tell your grasping younger son that every time he brings this up in the future, you'll deduct $1,200 from his share of the estate and divide it between Charles and his sister.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have two daughters, ages 19 and 21. They both have jobs. My husband and I would like them to help pay for a family vacation because they expect expensive experiences. Are we wrong to ask them to contribute? — <i>HELPING OUT IN NEW YORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR HELPING:</b> I don't think it would be wrong to enlighten your daughters about what the family vacation is costing. If their expectations will uncomfortably strain your budget, explain that you will need them to chip in so they can experience everything they want.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Key education endorsements for CPS School Board candidates
entries.summary: <p>Below are organizations that do education-related work that made endorsements in the 2026 Chicago School Board election. We also list education-focused political action committees that don’t endorse but are providing financial support to specific candidates. Election Day is Nov. 3.</p><p>We are not listing all endorsements, including from those from elected officials, from non-education organizations or those that aren’t directly tied to Chicago Public Schools. Those are available on each candidate’s website. Comprehensive information on each candidate is available at our voter guide.</p><p>Details on each group we included are below.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Teachers Union</u></b></a>: The largest union in Chicago Public Schools, including nearly 30,000 teachers, paraprofessionals, clinicians and school-related personnel, known for its strong focus on social justice issues.</p><p><b>Chicago Democrats for Education</b>: This political action committee was launched during the first school board election in 2024 to support “independent” candidates for the school board. The group was set up to be a counterbalance to the CTU and the mayor. It was formed by Hugo Jacobo, a heavyweight political consultant.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://cgcollective.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Common Ground Collective</u></b></a>: A new pro-business, anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.” The group says it wants to “defeat extremist efforts from both the far right and far left that seek to divide our city.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://incsaction.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>INCS Action PAC</u></b></a><b> for Public Charter Schools</b>: This political action committee is affiliated with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, which advocates on behalf of publicly funded, independently run charter schools. It is “focused on engaging the charter school community in the legislative and political process.” The group hasn’t made endorsements as of mid-September, but has donated to select candidates.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://wearelee.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Leadership for Educational Equity</u></b></a><b>, LEE PAC: </b>This organization and affiliated political action committee provides support and campaign services for reduced costs for alumni of education nonprofit groups, including Teach for America, New Leaders and School Board Partners, and other civic-minded organizations, that are running for public office. This group also donates under the name Leaders in Education.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://onepeoplescampaign.org/" target="_blank" ><b><u>ONE People’s Campaign</u></b></a><b>:</b> This grassroots campaign says it puts “the interests of regular people before the profits of corporations and the super rich” and focuses on supporting and endorsing progressive causes.</p><p><b>Our Schools Action:</b> This coalition of CTU-backed political groups and organizations backs progressives and leftist policies. Its affiliated <a class="Link" href="https://www.elections.il.gov/CampaignDisclosure/CommitteeDetail.aspx?ID=Hcp8Ad%2bsK%2f%2bv2F5OYMclfg%3d%3d" target="_blank" ><u>Our Schools</u></a> political action committee donated to a few school board candidates.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://seiu73.org/election-2026/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Illinois State Council</u></b></a><b>: </b>This union represents thousands of Chicago Public Schools support staff, including special education classroom assistants, security officers, bus aides, crossing guards and custodians. It has split politically with the Chicago Teachers Union in recent years. The CPS affiliate is SEIU Local 73.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://urbancenteraction.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>The Urban Center</u></b></a><b>:</b> This centrist political organization advocates for school choice across public and private schools and supports charter schools. It was founded before the first school board election in 2024 by Juan Rangel, a long-time operative in political and in education circles. It says its mission is “to support candidates in Chicago and across Illinois who back a common sense agenda that builds strong families, safe neighborhoods, world-class schools and greater economic opportunities.”</p><h3><b>Board president</b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-81b891d6-b2a9-11f1-9f14-f9252ebffa91"><li>Victor P. entries.title: How we made the CPS School Board voter guide
entries.summary: <p>To create the 2026 Chicago School Board voter guide we relied on our journalism skills and on you — voters, readers, listeners, parents and everyday Chicagoans.</p><p>First, the journalism part. We emailed a questionnaire to all candidates who filed to run in the school board election. Candidate responses were only edited to meet length requirements and to conform with our editorial style and commitment to refrain from publishing unsubstantiated statements. They were not edited for grammar or spelling. Candidate age is as of Sept. 1.</p><p>Biographical information was culled from candidate questionnaires, resumes, campaign websites and interviews. For race profiles published in the guide, reporters conducted interviews and background research on all candidates, including campaign finance data, educational credentials, lawsuits, criminal records, and business activity. Everything was fact-checked to the best of our abilities.</p><p>The endorsements we list only include organizations that do education-related work. We also list education-focused political action committees that don’t endorse but have singled out specific candidates for contributions. You can find more information <a class="Link" href="http://wbez.org/education/2026/09/17/key-education-endorsements-for-cps-school-board-candidates" target="_blank" >here</a>.</p><p>Now to the part about your role.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/12/08/few-residents-know-chicago-will-have-a-fully-elected-school-board-poll-finds" target="_blank" ><u>poll last year</u></a> showed two-thirds of Chicagoans didn’t know they could cast ballots for the city’s first-ever fully elected school board on Nov. 3. It doesn’t help that it’s confusing to find out which school board district you live in, and that this process is entirely new — to everyone.</p><p>So when we set out to make this voter guide, we didn’t just want to help you decide which candidate to vote for. We wanted to help you understand this new electoral process.</p><p>We wanted to make this <i>with </i>and <i>for </i>you. Here’s how we did it.</p><p>With our partners Chalkbeat Chicago and Block Club Chicago, we started by asking voters and Chicago Public Schools parents some questions: What educational issues do you care most about? What questions would you ask the school board candidates? What do you need to know about this new board?</p><p>We worked with dozens of local education groups — including Raise Your Hand, Kids First Chicago and the Parent Engagement Institute — who helped connect us with parents and understand their communities’ information needs.</p><p>More than 900 people responded from neighborhoods across the city, representing more than 260 CPS schools. Our survey wasn’t scientific, but clear themes emerged: In the classroom, people cared most about improving reading skills and preparing kids for life after graduation. For example, Torrence Winfrey of the South Side said in his survey that he wants CPS board members to “focus on vocational education for students where they graduate with real employable skills.” He wanted to ask candidates “what meaningful changes” they would initiate to “help kids create careers?"</p><p>Outside academics, people were passionate about equitably funding schools and making sure CPS is spending tax dollars efficiently.</p><p>They also posed tough questions to the candidates — about their relationships with the Chicago Teachers Union. About screen time and AI in classrooms. About chronic absenteeism.</p><p>We listened to what you told us. Your questions formed the backbone of the questionnaire we sent to all school board candidates who filed petitions to run, like the one from Lawanda Kelly of the Northwest Side, who asked about “the single most overlooked factor impacting instructional effectiveness in CPS classrooms.”</p><p>Some 43 candidates ultimately made it on the ballot, plus three declared write-ins.</p><p>You can read the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" >entire guide</a> in English and in Spanish online, as well as targeted voting districts in Chinese. We are also printing 30,000 copies to distribute around the city.</p><p>We are also planning a forum for the four school board president candidates on Oct. 14 at 8 pm on WBEZ 91.5. A video will also be available online at the same time. It will feature questions from an audience of Chicago Public Schools students — part of a larger effort to partner with CPS high school classes to increase news literacy for the next generation of voters.</p><p>Happy voting!</p>
entries.author: Alex Keefe

entries.title: What you need to know about Chicago’s historic school board election
entries.summary: <p>This fall, Chicagoans will vote for members of the city’s first fully elected school board. Every eligible Chicagoan can cast two votes (yes, two!) — one for a candidate in your school board district, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" >based on your home address</a>, and a second time for school board president.</p><h2><b>How can I vote in school board elections?</b></h2><p>All voters, whether they have students in Chicago Public Schools or not, can cast ballots in the school board elections.</p><p>They are on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. <a class="Link" href="https://ova.elections.il.gov/" target="_blank" ><u>Online voter registration</u></a> is available until Oct. 18 and same-day registration is allowed at the polls. <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/your-voter-information" target="_blank" ><u>Check your voter registration status here</u></a>. You must be 18 on election day, a U.S. citizen, and have lived at your current address for 30 days.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/early-votingvote-centers" target="_blank" ><u>Early voting</u></a> begins Oct. 1 at the Downtown Voting Supersite at 137 S. State St. and the Chicago Board of Elections Offices at 69 W. Washington St., 6th Floor.</p><p>Additional <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/early-votingvote-centers" target="_blank" ><u>early voting sites in all 50 wards</u></a> open Oct. 19. On Election Day Nov. 3, polls are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. Find your <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/your-voter-information" target="_blank" >assigned precinct polling place here</a>.</p><p><b>How many school board seats are up for election?</b></p><p>All 21 seats on the Chicago Board of Education are on the ballot. Each voter can pick their local representative on the board and the person they want to be school board president.</p><p>There are 43 candidates, plus three write-ins. Four people are running for school board president.</p><p>The city is divided into 20 electoral districts — 1a, 1b, etc.. You can look up which one you live in here. The president is elected citywide and will serve a four-year term until 2030.</p><p>When the new school board is seated in January, it will replace a board that is partially elected and partially appointed. That hybrid board, launched after elections in November 2024, was the first step toward the fully elected school board.</p><p>Half of the board members will serve four-year terms and the other half will serve two years. <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/documents/legislation/ilcs/documents/010500050K34-3.htm" target="_blank" ><u>Per state law</u></a>, members elected to replace mayoral appointees will serve two years, while those in districts that had elections in 2024 will serve four years. The term lengths will swap starting in 2028.</p><p><b>What does the school board do? </b></p><p>School board members are responsible for the education of about 315,000 children across more than 600 schools and set priorities for Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>Chicagoans are probably most familiar with one of the board’s core functions: making financial decisions. The school board can raise local property taxes and decide how to spend state and federal funding.</p><p>In the last year, the board stepped into new territory when it amended the budget prepared by CPS leaders, bucking their warnings. A narrow majority of members <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/12/cps-says-it-cannot-reverse-all-layoffs/" target="_blank" ><u>voted to rescind hundreds of staff layoffs</u></a> and instead build in a revenue assumption that Illinois lawmakers would provide <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" >$150 million more</a> than they had already allocated.</p><p>Another key board power is <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/30/chicago-board-of-education-hires-macquline-king/" target="_blank" ><u>hiring a CEO/superintendent</u></a> and later evaluating their performance.</p><p>The board also votes to close and open schools, the academic calendar, and on which buildings get upgrades. It also approves contracts, including collective bargaining agreements, and contracts with charter school operators.</p><p>In Chicago, the board now has power to gather <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/13/chicago-public-schools-board-backs-revenue-referendums/" target="_blank" ><u>community input through referendums</u></a>.</p><p>Board members are not paid.</p><h2><b>Why didn’t Chicago always vote for school board members?</b></h2><p>Since 1995, the mayor has appointed Chicago’s school board members. Before that, there was typically a nomination process to place members on the board.</p><p>Outside Chicago, most <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/02/17/nx-s1-5717076/americas-school-boards-in-2026" target="_blank" ><u>school boards in Illinois and across the U.S.</u></a> are elected.</p><p>But over the last two decades in Chicago, demand for an elected board grew with prominent organizations such as <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2021/7/30/22602068/illinois-governor-approves-elected-chicago-school-board/" target="_blank" ><u>the Chicago Teachers Union championing the change</u></a> to hold the board accountable to families and educators. Several decisions by the appointed board had soured public perceptions of the governing body, including its unanimous vote approving <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/06/13/chicago-public-schools-declining-enrollment-causes-small-schools-high-costs/" target="_blank" ><u>former Mayor Rahm Emanuel’s plan to close about 50 schools</u></a>.</p><p>The bill creating the elected school board <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2021/6/16/22537184/chicago-elected-school-board-bill-clears-hurdle-but-questions-remain/" target="_blank" ><u>passed in 2021</u></a>.</p><p>The implementation was rocky in Springfield and it faced <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2021/3/25/22351382/chicago-elected-school-board-bill-gains-momentum-calls-grow-for-another-option/" target="_blank" ><u>pushback from some local groups and former Mayor Lori Lightfoot</u></a> as it slowly got off the ground. As part of the path to a fully elected board, lawmakers required <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2024/09/25/cps-school-board-november-election-voter-guide-meet-the-candidates/" target="_blank" ><u>half the board to be elected</u></a> in 2024. The other half remained mayoral appointees, with the mayor retaining a majority.</p><p><i>Becky Vevea is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat Chicago. Makiya Seminera is a Chalkbeat reporter covering how the state and federal government affect education in Chicago and across Illinois. Emmanuel Camarillo is an education reporter for the Chicago Sun-Times.</i></p>

entries.title: Griffin MSI's new design must go back to the drawing board: 'Carbuncle in the park'
entries.summary: <p>The Griffin Museum of Science and Industry is one of those buildings that just looks good from all sides and angles — graced with perfect siting, courtesy of Daniel Burnham, and a great Greek Revival design by the hand of architect Charles Atwood.</p><p>The south side of the building is the winning view, of course, with that portico and the Columbia basin shimmering in front of it.</p><p>But the museum's primary elevation along 57th Street is the one everyone sees. It's an impressive neo-classical expanse behind a park-like front yard and punctuated by a colonnaded entry porch fit for the nobles of antiquity — or today's gaggle of school kids.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Alden Studios for RAMSA</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"The vision behind the Welcome Hall is to make the guest experience more accessible and enjoyable by creating a simpler path into the building while centering the historic facade as part of the arrival experience," the museum said in a statement.</p><p>But in doing so, the museum and its design firm RAMSA are expressing these noble goals with an ungainly and unattractive entry pavilion that visually overpowers the building's historic north entrance and its beautiful, open front lawn.</p><p>The building threatens to foul-up one of the city's great urban vistas — a remarkable blend of architecture, land, sky and history. One that looks just fine the way it is.</p><p>The whole thing should be sent back to the drawing board.</p><p>The museum and the Jackson Park green space it sits on so effortlessly came at great cost. And they belong to the public.</p><p>Built as the Palace of Fine Arts for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, and the fair's only surviving building, the edifice was saved from utter ruin by a $5 million effort — $130 million in today's money — that restored the structure and allowed it to reopen in 1933 as the Museum of Science and Industry.</p><p>The park in front of the museum was created in 1998 when a 6-acre surface parking lot — an eyesore if there ever was one — was replaced with a 1,500-space underground parking facility, costing nearly $120 million in current-day cash.</p><p>The garage gives drivers below-ground entrance to the museum, but its design also forces those who don't arrive by car to go down into the space to buy tickets, then take an escalator up into the museum.</p><p>The glass-faced Welcome Hall would link to the museum via a 124-foot glass connection that burrows straight through the center of the building's exterior stairs.</p><p>Visitors could still enter the museum through what remains of the stairs, but it's a little tough to see that historic rise of limestone just being gouged through like that.</p><div class="Enhancement" 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/93e1d0a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+2/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd5%2Fd3%2Fda539d624d64af229330ecb9a879%2Frs63163.jpg" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Welcome Hall would lead to a remodeled entry inside the museum.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Alden Studios for RAMSA</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>RAMSA's design puts a new glass wall behind the entry porch's columns and retains the existing stone wall that's behind them.</p><p>Granite floors are planned for the entry pavilion, and the building's metal arched roof would be planted with grass.</p><p>"The glass entryway and surrounding outdoor space will be free and open to everyone," the museum said. "Throughout the development of this project, Griffin MSI has been engaging with local community, accessibility and historic preservation groups and receiving feedback and support."</p><p>This is laudable. The museum and RAMSA are correct in wanting to create more free and accessible spaces and improve what is a cumbersome entry process.</p><p>But the proposed design can't be the only way to go about it.</p><p>The Permit Review Committee of the Commission on Chicago Landmarks approved the museum's plan on Sept. 10, agreeing with the assessment by the Department of Planning and Development's Historic Preservation Division that the Welcome Hall "will not have an adverse effect on the significant historical and architectural features of the landmark property."</p><p>I couldn't disagree more. The Welcome Hall is too tall and much too wide. It promises to sit there like a carbuncle in the park. And its arched grass roof makes the structure resemble a displaced section of Teletubbyland.</p><p>There's enough time, talent and cash on the table to develop something far better, given the design power of RAMSA — the late Robert A.M. Stern's successor firm — and whatever portion is left of hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2019/10/3/20896953/museum-of-science-industry-changing-name-125-million-gift-ken-griffin" >$124 million 2019 donation</a> to the museum that's still burning a hole in its pockets. </p><p>RAMSA's previously announced proposed South Portico <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/23/griffin-museum-science-industry-reopen-south-entrance-portico-after-century" target="_blank" >renovation plan</a> seems to be more appropriate and less monumental in approach, according to the latest renderings.</p><p>The Welcome Hall plan doesn't have to replicate that, but the design is some early evidence that a more sensitive approach on the north side is possible.</p><p>Approval from the landmarks commission and, ultimately, the Chicago City Council would be needed for the Welcome Hall to become a reality.</p><p>But the plan doesn't deserve to get that far. The museum and city landmarks officials must rethink this thing and come up with an approach that properly honors this world-famous building and its important site.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/23/griffin-museum-science-industry-reopen-south-entrance-portico-after-century" >Back door no more: Museum of Science and Industry seeks to reopen its south entrance after a century</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2019/10/3/20896953/museum-of-science-industry-changing-name-125-million-gift-ken-griffin" >Museum of Science and Industry changing name after $125M gift from Ken Griffin</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Push for independent review of Cook County Jail comes amid concerns over deaths, supervision
entries.summary: <p>Some Cook County commissioners are pushing for an independent review of the Cook County Jail, citing concerns about deaths, medical care and inadequate supervision.</p><p>A resolution calling for the review is scheduled for a vote Tuesday in the board's Health and Hospitals Committee.</p><p>Advocates, elected officials and faith leaders say the 2023 death toll — the deadliest year at the jail in decades — underscores the need for third-party oversight.</p><p>In 2023, 18 people died at the jail, many from drug overdoses tied to delays in medical care, according to an Injustice Watch investigation.</p><p>“I'm sponsoring the resolution because I'm concerned,” said Commissioner Tara Stamps. “We know that the detainees walked in alive and were unalive for whatever reason, and that one death is too many. And the numbers that we are looking at, in my opinion, require an outside review.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tara Stamps speaks during a 2022 news conference in which then-Cook County Commissioner Brandon Johnson announced he was running for mayor of Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Michele Deitch, director of the Prison and Jail Innovation Lab at the University of Texas at Austin, said such a review is standard in many large U.S. cities.</p><p>“New York, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Denver, San Diego, just to name a few, have some form of independent oversight over the jail facilities in that jurisdiction. So Chicago is unusual in not having it,” said Deitch.</p><p>Cook County Jail has had third-party oversight before.</p><p>Overcrowding and inadequate staffing led to federal court oversight of the jail complex on the Southwest Side in 1974.</p><p>In 2010, the jail entered into a new federal consent decree with the U.S. Department of Justice, following a 2008 report that gave the jail failing marks for the safety of inmates, medical care, sanitary conditions, fire safety and guards’ use of excessive force.</p><p>A federal judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/6/13/18373168/cook-county-jail-emerges-from-43-years-of-federal-oversight" target="_blank" >ended that oversight </a>in 2017 after ruling the jail had met reform requirements.</p><p>Stamps said she wants to bring back third-party oversight to the jail, though she added “the resolution does not accuse any individual, employee, office, or agency of wrongdoing, nor does it presume that the review will find any."</p><p>“The purpose is really just to establish reliable facts, identify any systemic concern and recognize practices that are working, and recommend improvements where they are warranted,” Stamps said.</p><p>Since 2023, deaths at the jail have trended downward, data shows. A spokesperson for the Cook County sheriff’s office said the majority of those deaths have been due to natural causes from medical issues or drugs.</p><p>“We have embraced new technologies, such as mail scanners, to stop the introduction of drug-soaked paper,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “We have added additional correctional staff to screen incoming mail and increase searches of the jail living units. We implemented drug testing to identify individuals in custody under the influence of drugs and promptly investigate individuals that are introducing illegal drugs and contraband into the jail.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-850000" name="image-850000"></a> <picture But Stamps said it’s not a “one-and-done deal.”</p><p>“This is the beginning of trying to create an ecosystem of care and compassion for the least of these detainees, which are often Black and brown men and women who find themselves in the care and custody of Cook County Jail," she added.</p><p>Deitch agrees lasting oversight is critical.</p><p>“The problems inside any jail, any prison system, any place of detention are chronic, meaning there are always going to be issues, and people inside are always going to be vulnerable,” she said.</p><p>“For that reason, we need to have ongoing, permanent, independent oversight of these places of detention. entries.title: After being charged by Illinois' special prosecutors, a lawyer and legal researcher unearthed misconduct
entries.summary: <p>In LaSalle County’s stately courthouse in central Illinois, a powerful law enforcement official fought a bitter legal feud with an unflappable young lawyer, charging her with felony perjury for statements she made in a court affidavit.</p><p>Two years later and 250 miles south in St. Clair County, a similar legal grudge match washed through the glass-and-concrete courthouse when a news researcher was charged with harassing a public official for alleged statements he made outside a local diner.</p><p>In both cases, the accusations were leveled by members of Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit — the elite squad of state lawyers who typically handle cases when local prosecutors have conflicts.</p><p>In their separate corners of the state, attorney Julie Ajster, 50, and court researcher Bradley VanHoose, 59, were acquitted of the felony charges they faced.</p><p>They then used their legal research skills to gather boxes of records on the special prosecutors who attacked them in court.</p><p>“I didn’t know what the Special Prosecution Unit was until I was charged,” VanHoose said. “That’s when I made it my life’s mission to find out everything I could about this agency.”</p><p>Injustice Watch independently verified these records and Ajster’s and VanHoose’s accounts, which reveal previously unreported misconduct and conflicts of interest by the Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/14/illinois-special-prosecution-unit-crime-politics" target="_blank" >An Injustice Watch investigation</a> showed the unit has faced accusations of ethical breaches, including withholding evidence and favoring political insiders, while <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/14/special-prosecutor-unit-illinois-politics-crime-mautino" target="_blank" >operating with little public oversight</a>.</p><p>The two veteran special prosecutors who indicted Ajster and VanHoose — Brian Towne in LaSalle County and David Rands in St. Clair County — shoulder some of the unit’s heaviest caseloads. Both also played leading roles in the unit’s problematic history.</p><p>VanHoose and Ajster had never met nor even heard about one another until a reporter shared their stories in recent interviews. They had independently reached out to Injustice Watch after it published its investigation last month.</p><p>“I’m glad I have another kindred spirit out there,” VanHoose said. “I know what the Special Prosecution Unit did to me was wrong. The charges against me were a politically based vendetta. Now, here’s another person who recognized this is wrong and stood up like I did.”</p><p>Towne and Rands did not respond to written questions about the findings. Patrick Delfino, who heads the agency that houses the unit — the Illinois State’s Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor, or ILSAAP — also did not respond to written questions.</p><h3><b>The small-town attorney</b></h3><p>Perhaps this all started because Ajster fell in love with a warehouse worker and stuck with him when he was badly injured working on a loading dock.</p><p>A lawyer from downstate Peru, she handled compensation cases for injured workers, crusaded against illegal puppy mills and was named one of Illinois Valley’s “40 Under 40” young business leaders.</p><p>In 2014, Towne charged Ajster’s fiancé Danny French with felony harassment by telephone for allegedly threatening an attorney who was a contributor to Towne’s political funds.</p><p>Those political connections bothered Ajster. “I didn’t know anything about Towne, but the case kind of pissed me off,” she said.</p><p>Towne, it turns out, wore many hats. While serving as LaSalle County state’s attorney in 2011, he created an unorthodox team of highway patrol officers who pulled over interstate drivers suspected of drug trafficking and confiscated whatever cash they were carrying. He called it the SAFE Team, short for State’s Attorney’s Felony Enforcement, and it grew as it confiscated more than $1 million from drivers during the five or so years it operated.</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Lawyer Julie Ajster</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Facebook</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ajster was recruited to represent drivers whose cash was seized by Towne’s team. Starting as early as 2012, lawyers said in court that Towne’s overlapping law enforcement roles created an obvious, disqualifying conflict: He was acting as both police and prosecutor, which is not permitted under Illinois law.</p><p>To resolve the issue, Towne began asking the court to bring in the Illinois Special Prosecution Unit to try SAFE Team cases in his stead. LaSalle County judges granted his requests.</p><p>But that only deepened Towne’s conflicts, Ajster later said in court. In 2012, Towne had become chairman of the board of governors that oversaw ILSAAP, the state agency that housed the Special Prosecution Unit. He was effectively in charge of the special prosecutors who were called in to replace him in the name of independence.</p><p>Ajster also discovered new details about financial ties between Towne’s SAFE Team and ILSAAP.</p><p>Starting in 2013, she found, ILSAAP paid the SAFE Team up to $40,000 a year to hire additional police officers. She also documented SAFE Team expenditures on a softball team sponsorship and a school trip that boosted Towne’s visibility as an elected state’s attorney; generous per diems for Towne’s junkets to Las Vegas law enforcement seminars; and his SUV, cellphone, team workout equipment and television monitors, according to receipts she filed in St. Clair County circuit court.</p><p>Meanwhile, as part of his prosecution of Ajster’s fiancé French, Towne took the unusual step of eavesdropping on Ajster.</p><p>One of French’s own friends was a key witness against him. The friend said French had bragged during a card game about threatening the lawyer. French’s friend then moved to Florida — in court papers, Ajster said this was to avoid testifying.</p><p>In 2015, Towne brought two Peru police officers to Tampa to eavesdrop on calls the friend placed with French and Ajster. Towne received LaSalle County court authorization for the surveillance.</p><p>According to Towne’s police report on one of the recorded calls, Ajster told her fiancé’s friend she was not going to tamper with the case and it was his choice whether to retract his previous statements.</p><p>“Several minutes into the conversation Danny French could be heard telling [the friend] to throw the statement away in the trash,” the police report said.</p><p>Towne secured a LaSalle County court order giving him 90 days to listen in on more phone calls if needed. It was only months later that Ajster learned she had been secretly recorded, when French and his lawyers received notice of the surveillance as part of discovery in his case.</p><p>Ajster rushed to the courthouse to find the orders authorizing the surveillance, but the clerk’s office said it had no such records.</p><p>“They didn’t even have a file on it because the orders were secret,” she said. “I thought I was living in the twilight zone. Like, this is America! This isn’t how the court system should operate. It’s what happens when people have unchecked control.”</p><p>Towne separately used a recorded call to disqualify Ajster from being French’s attorney — because she had now become a potential witness in his case.</p><p>And Towne charged Ajster with two felony counts of perjury, asserting a statement she made in a recorded call contradicted an affidavit she filed to reduce French’s bail.</p><p>The perjury charges against Ajster ultimately were dropped, but Towne filed a complaint with the Illinois Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission, which later found Ajster misrepresented French’s income to the court and suspended her license for 30 days — a conclusion Ajster calls unfair.</p><p>As the 2016 St. Clair County state’s attorney election approached, Ajster — and the revelations in her court records — fueled a “Dump Towne” campaign. Challenger Karen Donnelly unseated Towne, winning 54% of the vote.</p><p>Weeks later, Towne was hired as a member of the Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>Ajster said she was disappointed but not surprised to learn of Towne’s new law enforcement title.</p><p>But, in early 2017, LaSalle County news outlets reported Towne was the subject of a grand jury investigation, spurred by Ajster’s court filings about SAFE Team spending.</p><p>Then, in a separate case, the Illinois Supreme Court issued a biting decision, ruling Towne had acted outside his legal authority in creating and leading the SAFE Team.</p><p>Donnelly indicted Towne for official misconduct and misapplication of funds pertaining to SAFE Team expenses, most of which were first exposed by Ajster.</p><p>But Towne successfully petitioned the court to have a special prosecutor brought in to replace Donnelly since she had been his political opponent.</p><p>That courtroom tactic derailed the charges against Towne: When Donnelly appealed her disqualification, Towne’s lawyers filed a demand for a speedy trial — which meant the LaSalle County court had only 160 days to try him.</p><p>The newly appointed special prosecutor — retired Warren County judge Gregory McClintock — said he was forced to abandon the prosecution as the clock ran out.</p><p>Asked whether Towne should have been charged, McClintock said: “I would not proceed with a case where I didn’t think I had the evidence to prove somebody guilty.”</p><p>Ajster made one final attempt to hold Towne accountable. In 2018, she filed a federal malicious prosecution lawsuit against local police and won a $75,000 settlement. State’s attorneys such as Towne generally are immune from civil liability, but the judge ordered Towne to pay Ajster a symbolic $1.</p><p>“I settled with Ajster for one American dollar,” Towne told a news organization at the time. “In my mind, it was worth a buck to have Ajster out of my life.”</p><p>Ajster said she had the $1 bill framed and hung on the wall of her law office. But the episode rattled her faith in the law.</p><p>“I no longer refer to it as the justice system,” she said. “I refer to it as the legal system because there’s little to no justice in it.”</p><h3>The court researcher</h3><p>VanHoose was a Belleville high school jock who cut grass for a lawn service before he discovered his calling in court research.</p><p>He learned his craft tracking the torrent of asbestos lawsuits sluicing through Madison County, a national clearinghouse for plaintiffs’ claims. Colleagues described him as a hard-charging, meticulous researcher.</p><p>“I’m a good digger, and I’ll be honest with you — it’s what I should have been doing my whole life,” he said.</p><p>VanHoose is also well known around town as a lightning rod who maintains a frequent — sometimes vitriolic — presence on social media, posting about local and national politics.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Court researcher Bradley VanHoose, seen here in a 2019 Facebook post, made it his mission to learn everything he could about Illinois Special Prosecutor David Rands. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Facebook</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In 2016, special prosecutor David Rands charged VanHoose with threatening a former mayor of downstate Caseyville during a profanity-laced confrontation outside a diner. VanHoose and the former mayor were related by marriage, and they had argued publicly in the past. VanHoose was exonerated by an appellate court following a four-year legal battle.</p><p>VanHoose applied his research skills to Rands, sketching out a rough spreadsheet of Rands’ cases in St. Clair County. Then, he queried ILSAAP and the local state’s attorney for details on Rands’ assignments, digitized the data and compiled a cache of documents.</p><p>Rands consistently downgraded charges of drunken driving and sexual abuse against the relatives of politically powerful people, an analysis of VanHoose’s court records shows.</p><p>In the courthouses of St. Clair and other counties, Rands had garnered a nickname.</p><p>“They called him ‘Rollover Rands,’ ” VanHoose said. “If your mommy and daddy are somebody important down here, or you get the right attorney, get it into the appellate prosecutor’s hands. Rands would just basically roll over and let the case go. Like magic, the charges will be gone.”</p><p>Among those well-connected defendants were the son of an Illinois appellate judge who had faced alcohol-related driving charges in St. Clair County as well as in Missouri and Tennessee.</p><p>After Rands reduced their charges to minor infractions like improper-lane use, many of those defendants had their cases expunged, eliminating any public record of what Rands had done.</p><p>In cases that stretch from 2001 to today, it is often impossible to tell why Rands was appointed as special prosecutor in the first place — in documents referring cases to his office, the rationale was often left blank.</p><p>In one quarterly report, Rands wrote he was assigned to handle ordinance violations involving a strip club because it was a “high profile matter for State’s Attorney; causing a lot of upset on County Board.” Special prosecutors are supposed to be called in only when the local prosecutor has a real or perceived conflict of interest.</p><p>A similarly baffling assignment came in 2015, when then-33-year-old Blaine Zdybel was arrested at Belleville’s Skyview Drive-In movie theater for allegedly exposing himself and propositioning two boys in a restroom. Rands was appointed special prosecutor but never brought Zdybel to trial. The case is still listed as open on the docket of the St. Clair County circuit court clerk.</p><p>While the case dragged on unresolved, Zdybel was charged five times with child sex crimes in Horry County, South Carolina, with one conviction, two dismissals and two recent cases pending. He also pleaded guilty to indecent liberties with a minor in Pender County, North Carolina. He is a registered sex offender in both states.</p><p>Rands’ inactivity in the Belleville arrest meant Zdybel faced no justice or accountability in St. Clair County, no chance at court-mandated treatment and no registration on Illinois’ sex offender registry.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a
