class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>One of Bradley VanHoose’s hand-drawn spreadsheets tracking cases pursued by Illinois special prosecutor David Rands. Defendant names have been redacted.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Bradley VanHoose</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>One of Rands’ duties in St. Clair County was to review police-involved fatal shootings and make an independent determination of whether charges against the officer were appropriate.</p><p>ILSAAP plays a similar function in Cook County, where it has conducted 73 such reviews from 2016 to last year, never once overruling the Cook County state’s attorney’s decision not to charge.</p><p>Among the cases Rands cleared in St. Clair County was the 2016 shooting of 35-year-old Jason Stringer, an unarmed Black man, by an off-duty police officer in a Wal-Mart parking lot.</p><p>According to a police report, officer Christopher Heatherly, along with two other officers and a police dog, approached Stringer as he and his girlfriend walked out of the Wal-Mart. As Stringer ran to his car, Heatherly pinned Stringer’s girlfriend to the pavement, then shot into Stringer’s car, later saying he thought Stringer was trying to ram into them.</p><p>Rands cleared Heatherly, saying in a two-page letter to St. Clair County’s chief judge: “It is this office’s opinion that no criminal charges should be filed against the officer in this matter.”</p><p>But Rands’ letter omitted key information about Heatherly’s credibility found in other public records.</p><p>Heatherly “knew Mr. Stringer was considered to be armed and dangerous,” Rands wrote. But Stringer was not armed, and no weapon was retrieved at the scene, according to a 157-page Illinois State Police report. In a local news interview, Stringer’s girlfriend later disputed the police’s account and denied Stringer was trying to ram them with his car.</p><p>Before the Stringer shooting, Heatherly had worked at seven southern Illinois police departments in 15 years. He lost one job at the East St. Louis police department after a shooting the police chief there said was reckless and had endangered the life of another officer.</p><p>After Rands cleared him, Heatherly went on to be convicted of misuse of official information by a public official for disclosing personal information from police files, court records show.</p><p>Heatherly, now retired, said the Stringer shooting was justified. He is appealing his 2024 conviction. He said of his career, “I got on some bad departments. When you are a good police officer who wants to work hard, sometimes, when you come to a department that is not used to working hard, it ruffles feathers.”</p><p>VanHoose and Ajster still are reckoning with the fallout from the special prosecutors’ failed attempts to put them in prison. Both say they tapped their savings to clear their names and lost friends and even family amid the prosecutors’ attacks.</p><p>VanHoose says his 74-year-old father died in 2017 believing VanHoose had committed a felony.</p><p>“I didn’t even get to talk to my dad at the end of his life,” VanHoose said. “That’s what hardened my heart and got me in the courthouse digging.”</p><p>Rands and Towne remain mainstays of the Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>Between them, they handled 177 cases in 20 counties during 2024, the most recent year for which complete records were available.</p><div entries.title: Cook County Jail detainee apparently starts smoky mattress fire, injuring him and 10 guards
entries.summary: <p>Ten Cook County Jail staffers suffered smoke inhalation and were taken to hospitals after a detainee apparently lit a small mattress on fire at the jail Sunday afternoon. </p><p>About 3 p.m., correctional deputies responded to a small mattress fire that appeared to have been set by an individual in custody inside his cell on Tier 5A in the residential treatment unit, according to a statement from the Cook County sheriff's office. </p><p>Deputies quickly extinguished the fire and evacuated the individual in custody, who was the sole occupant of the cell, according to the statement. </p><p>As Chicago fire department firefighters extinguished the fire, it created heavy smoke so all individuals in custody on that tier and all other tiers on the fifth floor were evacuated as a precaution, the statement said. </p><p> The individual in custody inside the cell where the fire occurred was transported to a local hospital in good condition as a precaution, and ten correctional deputies who responded to the fire were also transported as a precaution to local hospitals, where their conditions had stabilized, the sheriff's office said. </p><p>The detainee has since been discharged from the hospital and cleared to return to the jail as well as all other evacuated inmates, according to the sheriff's office. </p><p>The cause of the fire is under investigation. <br></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyuhihk-l-o/" target="_blank" >Becky Vevea</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyuhihk-l-b/" target="_blank" >Makiya href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyuhihk-l-p/" target="_blank" >Kate Grossman</a></h5><h5></h5><p><b>Historic election</b>: This fall, Chicagoans will <a class="Link" Every eligible Chicagoan can cast two votes (yes, two!) — one for a candidate in your school board district, based on your home address, and a second for school board president.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: School board members are responsible for the education of about 315,000 children across more than 600 schools and set priorities for Chicago Public Schools. grid</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyuhihk-l-dy/" target="_blank" >Matt Moore</a></h5><p>With a strict no-phones policy, a heap of ethereal indie-folk-rock cuts and a set design that could convince someone they had an encounter of the third kind, singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers took fans off the grid for an emotional stop on her headlining arena tour at the United Center on Saturday.</p><p>Bridgers' legion surrendered their phones at the UC’s front gates to security, who also quickly sealed smartwatches and other devices in Yondr pouches.</p><p>She held court on two stages, one anchored by her nine-piece band and the other mostly reserved for more stripped-down arrangements. A gulf of adoring fans separated the two raised platforms, as thousands in the arena's seats watched with full attention — low-lit masses devoid of the white glow of a cellphone screen. All eyes were trained on the 32-year-old singer-songwriter.</p><p>Saturday marked the second of Bridgers' two-night stint at the United Center for her "Lost Tour." She delivered a stellar set that successfully took the quietness of her guitar-driven songs to flashy arena-headlining heights without sacrificing the intimacy she has become known for.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydyuhihk-l-dj/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What was the last truly no-phones performance you attended? entries.title: Gov. Pritzker opens up about his 80 lb. weight loss, use of GLP-1 — ‘I think it’s what I need to succeed’
entries.summary: <p>Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024-democratic-national-convention/2024/08/20/pritzker-jb-donald-trump-kamala-harris-democratic-national-convention-dnc-speech" >Gov. JB Pritzker delivered</a> one of the most high-profile political speeches of his life two years ago at Chicago’s Democratic National Convention.</p><p>But two years later, Pritzker, 61, said he’s astounded to see photographs and video of that moment.</p><p>Pritzker is for the first time revealing publicly that he’s lost 80 pounds with the help of a GLP-1 weight loss medication, with plans to lose more. The governor laid bare his previously undisclosed medical history in an hour-long interview with the Chicago Sun-Times, admitting the “food noise” is gone, with daily exercise and the injections fueling weight loss he didn’t think was possible.</p><p>“I honestly didn’t think about the fact that just two years ago at the Democratic convention, that I was 80 pounds heavier. I didn’t notice that except that now I’ve seen pictures or video of myself and now that I’ve had some success, I look in the mirror and I think about the videos and I think, ‘Wow, that’s quite a difference,’” Pritzker said. “And I guess other people see it, which is nice.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-600000" name="image-600000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bd63a2d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5537x3108+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2Ff9%2Fa99686e34451aeb792d9ea7eaaef%2F2167657011.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c68beee/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5537x3108+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2Ff9%2Fa99686e34451aeb792d9ea7eaaef%2F2167657011.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fc4c28a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5537x3108+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2Ff9%2Fa99686e34451aeb792d9ea7eaaef%2F2167657011.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker speaks on stage during the second day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center Aug. 20, 2024 in Chicago." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fc4c28a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5537x3108+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2Ff9%2Fa99686e34451aeb792d9ea7eaaef%2F2167657011.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8f6dc93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5537x3108+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2Ff9%2Fa99686e34451aeb792d9ea7eaaef%2F2167657011.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fc4c28a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5537x3108+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F17%2Ff9%2Fa99686e34451aeb792d9ea7eaaef%2F2167657011.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker speaks on stage during the second day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center Aug. 20, 2024 in Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joe Raedle/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>For people who think Pritzker, a billionaire, has little to complain about — he has always battled with his weight.</p><p>“There are people who have it very easy their whole lives, and they’ve never struggled at all,” Pritzker said. “And I’m just not that person.”</p><p>Pritzker credits it in part to “bad genes.” He’s also been the target of weight-related attacks and AI-generated memes shared by President Donald Trump — including fake images of him devouring pizza and a burger. Trump has also repeatedly called him a “fat slob,” a reference the governor certainly remembers.</p><p>“I think that it's funny to me now that the president still calls me a fat slob… and I wasn’t before, by the way. But I’ve been overweight. Oh by the way, he’s overweight,” Pritzker said. “But I don’t really talk about that publicly… and it’s because I think it’s more like the content of your character that matters more, and I’ve always believed that. And that’s why I haven’t listened to people who say nasty things about me being overweight.”</p><p>He says he’s been on “every diet you could imagine” with no long-term success. But it wasn’t until a doctor diagnosed him with pre-diabetes, and later Type II diabetes, at age 58 that he began taking insulin — and ultimately a GLP-1 medication to help regulate his blood sugar.</p><p>Pritzker calls it a “miracle” that he didn’t have health problems prior to that moment.</p><p>“I’ve been testing myself regularly like people do when they go to the doctor. Maybe I would do it once a year, and never have any problems. It’s almost a miracle, really,” Pritzker said. “If you think about the number of years being overweight — no glucose problem, no other problems.”</p><p>It was that diabetes diagnosis and insulin prescription that gave him a life-saving wake-up call — and got him thinking about his own longevity.</p><p>Pritzker said the medication — combined with exercise and diet — has been so efficient that he stopped taking insulin nine months ago, and his blood sugar levels have gone back to normal.</p><p>The Democratic governor’s weight loss has been gradual — noticeable. In the early days, his suits sometimes looked like they were hanging off his body. He has since upgraded his smaller sized wardrobe.</p><p>He’s also frequently spotted walking several miles along Lake Michigan in the mornings — and he’s taken hundreds of questions about his weight, each time crediting his weight loss to his new exercise routine and declining to answer whether it was also fueled by a GLP-1 medication. He repeatedly called it a “private health matter.”</p><p>But more than two years into his new weight loss journey, the governor said he wants to talk about it openly, largely in part because he knows millions of Americans are suffering from obesity-related health conditions. And he says he didn’t talk about it sooner because he wanted to make sure the weight loss stuck. The disclosure also comes just months before Democrats are expected to announce their intentions to run for president.</p><p>For now, the governor won’t take the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/09/pritzker-for-president-handicapping-the-illinois-governors-political-future" > presidential bait </a>and said he’s focusing on winning his third term for governor in November.</p><p>“People want to tag that, but I mean really, really honestly… I might not be on a GLP-1 had I not walked into that doctor’s office or gotten that call, and so that really is what put me on the GLP-1,” Pritzker said. “And the fact that I’m losing weight, frankly, I would like to be around to have my children have children. So I can have grandchildren.”</p><h3><b>The role his family health plays</b></h3><p>Pritzker’s tragic childhood included the deaths of both his parents — his mother <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/13/23069709/gov-jb-pritzker-mother-sue-abortion-rights-family-legacy-national-leadership-roe-v-wade-alcoholism" target="_blank" >Sue killed in a gruesome car accident when he was 17,</a> and his father Donald, who died of a heart attack at age 39, when Pritzker was just seven.</p><p>And that number — 39 — is something the Pritzker family, including the governor’s sister Penny and brother Tony, thinks about — especially since they’ve made it well past that young age.</p><p>Pritzker said his father had high cholesterol, high triglycerides and high blood pressure. He said the family was always aware that there was a genetic possibility that one of them could suffer from alcoholism, as his mother did, although none did.</p><p>He said he paid attention “to not drinking too much,” but he wasn’t overly concerned about his heart health, because his bloodwork results were consistently normal.</p><p>The governor was extremely candid about his relationship with food — describing himself as the guy who wants the whole cake, not just a piece.</p><p>“It’s still a struggle. It used to be that somebody would say, ‘We’ve got cake’ or something and to me and I think to other people, but for me anyway, if you put a cake down and say, ‘Would you like some cake?’ Yeah, I want the whole cake or a box of cookies,” Pritzker said. “...That was just how I would feel about it, and I don’t feel that way anymore. I still like — who doesn’t love cake and cookies. I love them, but I don’t feel like I need to have more than one, and most often I'm thinking, ‘I don't want to do that because I want to lose weight tomorrow.’”</p><p>The food noise is gone, he said, crediting the medication.</p><p>“I really don’t walk around thinking when is the next time I need to or that I get to eat,” Pritzker said. “Now, it’s much more normal.”</p><h3><b>State insurance covers Pritzker’s GLP-1 use </b></h3><p>Pritzker, who started his injections in the spring of 2024, said his weight loss medication is covered by the state’s insurance plan — but it’s attributable to his previous diabetes diagnosis, not specifically for weight loss.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/04/30/weight-loss-drug-coverage-illinois-state-workers-taxpayers-price-tag" >Illinois expanded coverage</a> for eligible state workers for medications like Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, in July 2023 under the state’s group health insurance program. The state’s expanded coverage cost the state $147 million in fiscal year 2025.</p><p>GLP-1 coverage was previously available for state workers who had been diagnosed with diabetes — but the expansion covered the drug for weight loss, with more drugs available.</p><p>“I put that policy in place before I ever thought I’d be on a GLP-1. Just want to be clear. I’m not trying to, I wasn’t trying to do something for myself here,” Pritzker said. “It really was a policy decision.”</p><p>Pritzker has defended the inclusion of the weight-loss injections into the state’s insurance plan, calling it “good for the taxpayers” for its ability to get diabetics off of insulin.</p><p>“We brought down the cost of insulin for people long before we ever got to GLP-1s, but this actually allows people to — well I’m living proof that you can come off of them,” Pritzker said.</p><p>Despite praise for the drug’s effectiveness, the governor said he can’t rule out future cuts to coverage of the medication for weight loss due to budgetary constraints, saying, “of course virtually everything these days is on the table.”</p><p>“There are lots of things I don't like having to do these days that we shouldn’t have to do, but they’re being forced upon us,” Pritzker said. ”And so, is that on some very long list of things we would have to consider? Possibly. But I really haven’t contemplated it until you just asked the question.”</p><p>The governor said expansion of the weight loss drugs to Medicaid recipients, however, is not currently feasible.</p><p>“We have so many other things that we need to do with dollars in the Medicaid system that I can’t imagine that this would be immediately something we could do, given all the circumstances of the federal government,” Pritzker said, “But I would love to do that. I mean, it’s not like people who are lower income don’t have exactly the same problems. It’s not like the Medicaid system couldn’t benefit.”</p><h3><b>‘I don’t think it’s cheating’ </b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-860000" name="image-860000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dceefe3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6196x3477+0+327/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F39%2Fb9dc877c4969a5419d8241556507%2Fpritzkerinterview-260921-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/576c982/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6196x3477+0+327/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F39%2Fb9dc877c4969a5419d8241556507%2Fpritzkerinterview-260921-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9d57c73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6196x3477+0+327/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F39%2Fb9dc877c4969a5419d8241556507%2Fpritzkerinterview-260921-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Joggers talk to Gov. J.B. Pritzker at 31st Street Beach on the South Side as he was walking by, Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9d57c73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6196x3477+0+327/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F39%2Fb9dc877c4969a5419d8241556507%2Fpritzkerinterview-260921-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ce32392/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6196x3477+0+327/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F39%2Fb9dc877c4969a5419d8241556507%2Fpritzkerinterview-260921-3.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9d57c73/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6196x3477+0+327/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F39%2Fb9dc877c4969a5419d8241556507%2Fpritzkerinterview-260921-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Joggers talk to Gov. J.B. Pritzker at 31st Street Beach on the South Side as he was walking by Sept. 16.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>On a drizzly September morning, Pritzker took a morning walk near 31st Street Beach. He was immediately spotted and chatted with two runners and later with two bird watchers from the The Nature Conservancy and Windy City Bird Lab.</p><p>Beyond the Lake Michigan walks, Pritzker says he’s using a recumbent bike in his office on rainy days, and also using a treadmill, elliptical machines and whatever is available at hotel gyms. He’s also hiking with his son and playing tennis with his daughter.</p><p>Pritzker defended his use of a GLP-1 drug and said it isn’t a shortcut or “like steroids for sports figures.” He is crediting it as the biggest difference maker in his lifelong quest to lose weight.</p><p>“I feel so much better than I have in a long time. I’m able to do things I haven’t done in a long time. So, if there is this new opportunity to get healthy and in my case, it was driven by a true medical condition diagnosis… I don’t think it’s cheating,” Pritzker said. “I think it’s what I need to succeed.”</p>

entries.title: Naperville man, 70, fatally shot in Greater Grand Crossing
entries.summary: <p>A 70-year-old Naperville man who was looking for homes to flip was fatally shot in Chicago's Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood Saturday.</p><p>A homeowner called 911 about 10:15 a.m. Saturday when they noticed a vehicle parked in the alley, blocking their garage and couldn't get out in the 7000 block of South Calumet Avenue, according to a police report. </p><p>Responding officers found the unidentified 70-year-old, slumped over the driving wheel of his truck, shot in the head, police said. A single shell casing from a 9mm gun was found in the passenger's seat.</p><p>Police then recovered video nearby that showed an "unknown male" exit the victim's vehicle at about 8:15 p.m. Friday and walk away.</p><p>A relative of the 70-year-old said he was in the area looking for homes to flip, according to the report. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating. <br></p>

entries.title: Which Cubs and White Sox made it? Which didn't? We present the Sun-Times' 2026 All-City Team
entries.summary: <p>It’s time for both sides of this great baseball town to come together.</p><p>No, not the fans. We know better than to ask for that.</p><p>Rather, we mean the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> themselves, for — a doff of the cap and a drumroll, please — the Sun-Times’ 2026 All-City Team is here.</p><p>Beat writers Vinnie Duber (Cubs) and James Fegan (Sox) joined frequent baseball scribe Jeff Agrest and yours truly in selecting a 17-man team: one player at each position in the field, a designated hitter, four starting pitchers, three relievers — one of them designated as closer — and a manager.</p><p>Four ironclad rules guided our process:</p><p>1. This is a 2026 honor. Reputation doesn’t matter.</p><p>2. If it’s too close to call at certain positions, lean into which players we’d rather write into a playoff lineup.</p><p>3. All players must appear at their primary positions. No exceptions!</p><p>4. OK, fine, Alex Bregman and Miguel Vargas both need to be in there somehow. Besides, if we journalists followed the rules, how would everybody know to hate us?</p><p>Our team:</p><h3><b>SP1: Sean Burke, Sox</b></h3><p><i>Leads Chicago starters in ERA, strikeouts, opponent batting average — closest we’ve got to an ace.</i></p><h3><b>SP2: Shota Imanaga, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>Other than the gopher balls — so many gopher balls — lefty has been effective.</i></p><h3><b>SP3: Davis Martin, Sox</b></h3><p><i>Sox were 10-1 over his first 11 starts. Finishing kick has been strong, too. (As for in between, don’t ask.)</i></p><h3><b>SP4: Matthew Boyd, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>Still one guy who — if locked in — can get you to the seventh inning of a playoff game.</i></p><h3><b>C: Carson Kelly, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>Good hitter, even better with men in scoring position. Not an All-Star, but we’ll take him.</i></p><h3><b>1B: Munetaka Murakami, Sox</b></h3><p><i>Hamstring injury derailed spectacular start. Still, top 10 in AL in homers, walks is big-time.</i></p><h3><b>2B: Chase Meidroth, Sox</b></h3><p><i>Sorry, Nico Hoerner, but this was an easy call. Meidroth has simply been the better batsman.</i></p><h3><b>3B: Alex Bregman, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>One of the best second halves in baseball, combined with stellar glove work. Tough call, though.</i></p><h3><b>SS: Dansby Swanson, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>Just too great on “D” — and Colson Montgomery didn’t get on base enough to unseat him.</i></p><h3><b>LF: Tristan Peters, Sox</b></h3><p><i>South Side’s best outfielder — an All-Star, don’t forget — gets bumped over by you-know-who.</i></p><h3><b>CF: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>But you knew this already. Not bad, Mr. MVP.</i></p><h3><b>RF: Seiya Suzuki, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>His RISP work wasn’t the best, but you take the offensive totals every time.</i></p><h3><b>DH: Miguel Vargas, Sox</b></h3><p><i>Sox’ MVP — there’s no debate about that — simply has to be in our lineup.</i></p><h3><b>RP: Bryan Hudson, Sox</b></h3><p><i>Quality lefty with multiple impressive scoreless streaks and pinpoint control all second half.</i></p><h3><b>RP: Sean Newcomb, Sox</b></h3><p><i>Lefty hangs on to a spot despite a rough September.</i></p><h3><b>Closer: Grant Taylor, Sox</b></h3><p><i>The best reliever in town and the only sane choice for this role.</i></p><h3><b>Manager: Craig Counsell, Cubs</b></h3><p><i>Potentially winning 90 despite one pitching problem after another is nothing to sneeze at.</i></p><h3><b>DISSENSIONS IN THE RANKS</b></h3><p>In the end, we were in unison on all but three positions. Fegan backed Vargas at third base and Will Venable at manager, and I wanted Sam Antonacci in left.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Vargas has been the rock of a Sox offense otherwise defined by streaks. He’s the proof of concept of their newfound ability to improve hitters. A universally beloved bilingual glue guy in a loose clubhouse, Vargas is the team MVP who laughs hard and works harder. Without him, Sox leadership is talking “meaningful progress” rather than playoffs.</p><p><b>Greenberg on Antonacci: </b>His defense is more mosh pit than ballet, but throw him off his spot because of it? Come on, man. He’s always on base, hits in the clutch and plays with his rear end on fire. How do you not love a young cat with a perverse desire to stand in front of 96 mph and get drilled by it? entries.title: Review: Alanis Morissette, queen of confessional songwriting, recrowned for a new generation at Riot Fest
entries.summary: <p>When Carole King sang about feeling the earth move in 1971, she was prophesying the moment 55 years later when her songwriting descendant Alanis Morissette would take over Douglass Park and bring more than tens of thousands of people together to sing “you, you, you oughta know” from the depths of their jagged little hearts.</p><p>It was one of the most powerful moments of the Riot Fest 2026 weekend, and yes, underneath the soggy abyss, you could feel the ground shift a little with the weight of the crowd all moving together in the moment.</p><p>Many sacrifices were made to get to Morissette’s set Sunday night: Shoes were surrendered to the mud. People forfeited seeing William Shatner, whose set was pushed back after weather delays and the “Star Trek” actor was rebooked at the same time. And a good amount of sanity was abandoned after dealing with a full day of rain with attendees trenching through the thick sludge and going nowhere fast. It’s almost like Morissette wrote an “Ironic” song forecasting this very moment, too. Yet to see her fully command the stage with the opening harmonica swing of “Hand In My Pocket” to “All I Really Want” and all the songs that have become a lifeline for many over the years, it was worth it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-df0000" name="image-df0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-credit"><p>Rachel Zyzda</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Released in 1995, Morissette’s magnum opus “Jagged Little Pill” still resonates 30 years later. It’s a young woman’s guide to living that’s been passed down from mothers to daughters, aunts to nieces and older to younger sisters. At this point, it would be easier to find a group of people that Morissette hasn’t influenced. Not just casual fans either, but nearly all of the current Top 40.</p><p>Taylor Swift has sung her praises. So has PINK, Katy Perry and Halsey. Three weeks ago, Morissette was the surprise guest at Olivia Rodrigo’s inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Festival where the godmother of confessional songwriting was recoronated for a new generation.</p><p>There are few cultural figureheads that have continued to impact the zeitgeist like Morissette, with Riot Fest just adding one more notch on the timeline.</p><p>The hourlong set (which was dedicated to New Found Glory guitarist Chad Gilbert who passed away Sunday after a battle with cancer) started with a barrage of ephemera from the archives. Video screens scrolled through an endless amount of magazine clippings, late-night show tapings, iconic music videos and charged interviews where the then-young Canadian singer-songwriter was vehement about her stances on feminism, sexism and the undue pressures on Gen X. It was an effective setup to transport you back into the mind frame of the era when her works first came out and, sadly, to realize little has changed. Morissette pointed this out too.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3d0000" to endure early on — alarming statistics started popping up on the video screens. “81% of women reported some form of sexual harassment in their lifetime,” read one. “On average, women make 68% of what men make for the same work,” read another. “More than 120 million girls around the world have experienced sexual violence,” the scroll continued, later adding, “women experience high rates of depression, anxiety, PTSD and eating disorders.”</p><p>These are all, sadly, experiences Morissette had as a teen, which inspired the bulk of “Jagged Little Pill.” Over the years, she’s continued to remain open about it all, and in so doing, she has kept these important conversations going and brought it into the modern day. She and “Juno” writer Diablo Cody created the Tony Award-winning “Jagged Little Pill” musical doing the same, where they personified each of the songs within a storyline that tackled current affairs.</p><p>Morissette and the solid rock band behind her (which once featured the late Taylor Hawkins) also added a few other catalog hits to the set, like the haunting “Uninvited” and the sweet “Thank U.” But it was the “Jagged Little Pill” moments that really took on new life and made you hope Morissette keeps the heartbeat alive 30 years from now, too.</p><h3>Alanis Morissette set list for Sept. 20, 2026, show at Riot Fest</h3><p>Hand in My Pocket<br>Right Through You<br>Hands Clean<br>Head Over Feet<br>You Learn<br>Smiling<br>Ironic<br>All I Really Want<br>You Oughta Know<br>Uninvited<br>Thank U</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/20/photos-william-shatner-patti-smith-pennywise-sincere-engineer-largemouth-riot-fest-day-3" >Photos: Insane Clown Posse, Patti Smith, William Shatner, Pennywise, Sincere Engineer, Largemouth on Riot Fest Day 3</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/20/riot-fest-day-3-douglass-park" >Riot Fest Day 3: William Shatner, Patti Smith deliver inspiring sets on final day of the festival</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Cubs hit final week of wild-card race, Pete Crow-Armstrong nears 40-40 season: Playoff heroics next for MVP?
entries.summary: <p>Baseball’s a team sport.</p><p>There are 26 guys on the roster and a lot of things that need to go right in order to ensure victory and a run to a championship.</p><p>But while it takes a lot of contributors to win a World Series, having the game’s best player – in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ case, MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong – among them ain’t too shabby.</p><p>“He affects the game in every aspect,” designated hitter Michael Conforto said of his teammate last week. “Every time he comes up to the plate, he can change the score. If they don’t want to pitch to him, a walk is, a lot of times, going to be a double [because of his base-stealing ability]. He’s going to be on second base. And if they hit the ball anywhere in the middle of the field in the air, odds are he’s going to catch it.</p><p>“He’s really, in a big way, brought us to this point. And we’ve done a lot of great things to cover everything else, but Pete’s been a huge reason we’re in the position that we’re in.”</p><p>With six games remaining on the regular-season schedule, Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs have a decisive week ahead.</p><p>The 24-year-old center fielder is two stolen bases away from the seventh 40-homer, 40-steal season in baseball history. It would be the top line of an MVP resume already strong enough to earn him the award; he’s been far ahead in that race, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/05/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp-race-dodgers-playoffs-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga" >even of Dodgers two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani</a>, for months.</p><p>But Crow-Armstrong has made it clear that the individual accomplishments aren’t of much concern to him, especially compared to what it means for his team to achieve the goal it’s harbored since the spring.</p><p>Just one win in their final half dozen games will secure the Cubs’ place in the postseason. Even if they end up on the wrong end of sweeps against the Marlins and Red Sox, though, just one loss by the Diamondbacks will do the trick.</p><p>But where the Cubs play their opening-round playoff series remains very much in question.</p><p>They’re tied with the Padres for the NL’s No. 1 wild-card spot and just a game ahead of the Phillies. That the Cubs own the tiebreaker over both teams is helpful in landing a best-of-three wild-card series at Wrigley Field.</p><p>But even scoreboard-watching fans figure to be locked into what magic Crow-Armstrong can cook up as the regular season comes to a close and the Cubs look to advance deep into October.</p><p>A 40-40 season would be something wildly rare in baseball history, though it would be the third in the last four years after Braves star Ronald Acuna Jr. went 41-73 in 2023 and Ohtani went 54-59 in 2024.</p><p>But even with that recency, it would electrify the North Side, something Crow-Armstrong has made a habit of as he’s delivered MVP moments all season long.</p><p>“It is really similar to what I saw last year,” said Conforto, who was Ohtani’s Dodgers teammate in 2025. “You see a guy go out there and do things that no one else can do. And he does it different than Shohei does it. But it’s the same thing. He moves differently. He has different tools than everyone else.</p><p>“You just kind of enjoy sitting back and watching history being made.”</p><p>But that’s this week.</p><p>Come next Tuesday, when the wild-card round gets underway, a 40-40 season won’t mean as much to Crow-Armstrong if he can’t help the Cubs to the most important wins of their season.</p><p>Fortunately for the Cubs, he hasn’t slowed down, and that means they could be in for a full October’s worth of Crow-Armstrong highlights – with, they hope, a trophy presentation at month’s end.</p><p>“You look at the great teams in our sport – and I guess in sports, in general – there usually is a real superstar talent at the heart of it,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said. “I don’t think we need him to be superhuman in order to be successful, but it sure helps when he is.</p><p>“He’s had many games this year where he’s kind of won games single-handedly. … It’s hard to picture where we’d be this year without him.”</p>

entries.title: One dead in West Pullman shooting
entries.summary: <p>Police are investigating a fatal shooting Monday morning in West Pullman. </p><p>About 8:30 a.m. the unidentified victim, only described as male, was found in the 800 block of West 117th Street, police said in a statement. </p><p>The gunshot victim, who suffered multiple wounds, was dead on the scene and nobody else was hurt, police siad. </p><p>Circumstances surrounding the killing are under investigation by Area 2 detectives. </p>

entries.title: Review: Joffrey’s cinematic ‘Liliom’ enthralls, even if its complexities tangle audiences
entries.summary: <p>One of Rodgers and Hammerstein’s most memorable creations was the 1945 Broadway musical “Carousel.” The tragic, violence-tinged love story between a Maine millworker named Julie and the flawed carousel barker Billy Bigelow ends on a redemptive, upbeat note.</p><p>Almost forgotten is that the beloved musical was based on “Liliom,” a once well-known 1909 play by Hungarian playwright <a class="Link" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferenc_Moln%C3%A1r" target="_blank" >Ferenc Molnár</a>. And it is <a class="Link" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferenc_Moln%C3%A1r" target="_blank" >Molnár</a>’s darker, more complex tale that forms the basis of an intense ballet of the same name by the now 87-year-old American choreographer John Neumeier.</p><p>The Joffrey Ballet opened its 2026-27 season Thursday evening with the Chicago premiere of this nearly two-and-a-half hour work, which debuted in 2011 at the Hamburg Ballet. Neumeier, a Milwaukee native, served as director and chief choreographer of the German company from 1973 to 2024.</p><p>This audacious, highly imaginative adaptation shifts the setting to an American amusement park called Playland, setting the action against the bleak, sociopolitical backdrop of the 1930s Great Depression. In one ensemble scene, desperate unemployed men scuffle over a few job postings, scrambling over homeless figures sprawled on the ground.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div 7:30 p.m. Sept. 18 with eight more performances through Sept. 27<br><b>Where:</b> Lyric Opera House, 20 N. Wacker<br><b>Info:</b> (312) 386-8905 or<a class="Link" href="https://joffrey.org/performances-and-tickets/26-27-season/liliom/?gclsrc=aw.ds&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24128638795&gbraid=0AAAAADnc7R8IG3wx5XCEWoDXd0455geF9&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHRRupkBSVkQ0fpPHFuoeuZ3wb4Nx4UOcfUuaOK1MDjN266VbiCmkoxoC1U4QAvD_BwE" target="_blank" > joffrey.org</a>; tickets are $39-$214</div> </div><p>This version retains the name, Liliom, for the cocky, attention-grabbing carousel barker. Inescapably drawn to him is Julie, who in this version is a modest cafe waitress. Theirs is a troubled relationship with Liliom even hitting her in a fit of anger. Fired from his job and desperate for money, he commits a very public suicide after a botched robbery attempt and must face a kind of posthumous trial in what the ballet’s synopsis calls the “beyond.”</p><p>The ballet opens and closes 16 years after Liliom’s death with Playland closed and dilapidated. After serving time in purgatory, the barker is given a chance to redeem himself. He brings a star from heaven to his son, Louis, born after his death, but he fails in his mission to connect and lashes out at the teenager after being rejected.</p><p>Neumeier uses an overall dance vocabulary rooted solidly in ballet but draws here on Broadway show choreography and social dances, leaning into the theatrical expressionism inherent in Ferenc’s original play. This is especially true in his surreal depiction of a kind of trial in the afterlife with a gatekeeper (Dylan Gutierrez) and six red-suited devils, all moving in weirdly jerky, iterative ways.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Cheryl Mann</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Liliom” is also expressionist in the enthralling, often unsettling scenes that Neumeier interweaves into the main story. Carnival figures such as the Sad Clown (poignantly realized by Jackson Miles) constantly reappear, as do Chinese jugglers, with reminders of the larger world around the realm of Playland.</p><p>The ballet opens daringly in complete silence as the mysterious Balloon Man (Evan Boersma), holding a bunch of several dozen balloons in one hand, gradually makes his way across the stage with very long, outstretched strides as he sets about bringing Liliom momentarily back to earth.</p><p>The constant, unexpected juxtapositions in the ballet are echoed and extended in Michel Legrand’s wonderfully vibrant score that unexpectedly sets the Frank Sinatra panache of Rob Parton’s Jazztech Big Band against the Lyric Opera Orchestra, capably led Thursday evening by Nicholas Koo. (Read more here about<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/09/18/liliom-joffrey-ballet-michel-legrand-score-john-neumeier-dance-music-orchestra-jazz" target="_blank" ><u> the music</u></a> and how it is performed.)</p><p>Before his death in 2019, Legrand has wrote more than 200 television and film scores, so it’s not surprising that the music here has a definite cinematic flair with tinges of Aaron Copland and Leonard Bernstein.</p><p>If there is a downside to “Liliom,” the story can sometimes be difficult to follow even with the synopsis, and some of the emotional depth gets lost at times amid the work’s sheer narrative and theatrical complexity.</p><p>That said, the performances are uniformly superlative. José Pablo Castro Cuevas vividly embodies first the swagger and braggadocio of Liliom and later his pain, anger and shame. He is ideally matched with the ever-reliable Joffrey star, Victoria Jaiani, who manages to convey both Julie’s modesty and her attraction to the barker.</p><p>Marie (Natali Taht), a friend of Julie, and Wolf (Jonathan Dole), a hapless bellman, are kind of side characters in this story. But their duet is a joy, with the couple’s fresh, wholesome love expressed in simple movements like jogging arm in arm.</p><p>Providing a sharp contrast is another more suggestive duet early on between Liliom and his past lover, Mrs. Muscat, who owns the carousel where he was employed. Amanda Assucena aptly captures her scheming ways as she tries to lure him back, the two posturing and preening, with him flipping her over his back and onto his lap.</p><p>Overall, every Joffrey dancer smartly executes the unusual technical demands of Neumeier's ballet movement, while conveying the essence of their characters often through simple telling gestures.</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams has avoided serious hamstring injury
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/20/bears-vikings-caleb-williams-hurt-on-non-contact-play-nfl" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> seemed to have avoided a worst-case scenario.</p><p>The MRI tests the Bears sent him for Monday didn't show a significant injury.</p><p>"It sounds it's going to be a week-to-week deal," Bears coach Ben Johnson told play-by-play announcer Jeff Joniak on the team's official Monday coach's interview show on ESPN1000. </p><p>Johnson said he will "likely miss some time."</p><p>In the past, "week-to-week" has been Johnson's wording for an injury that doesn't require a trip to injured reserve. Whether Williams plays Monday night against the Eagles is a different question, though perhaps the Bears wouldn't mind giving their opponent something else to think about in the three days before they have to submit their first injury report to the league Thursday.</p><p>Tyson Bagent would start in Williams' place.</p><p>Williams hurt his hamstring on a first-down run midway through the fourth quarter in Sunday's 9-3 loss to the Vikings. He walked through the locker room on his own after the game and was in good spirits. Johnson said Sunday he was relieved that Williams didn't injure his knee when he fell to the ground on the non-contact play. </p><p>Bagent replaced Williams for two drives — one that started at the Bears' 6 and ended in a blocked field goal and another in which he drove the team to the Vikings' 12 in the final minute before being sacked as time expired. He last started a game during his rookie year in 2023. <br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Nothing is guaranteed, but Will Venable thinks the White Sox organization will only go up from here
entries.summary: <p>Will Venable was the associate manager on the 2023 Rangers team that won the World Series, and also of the 2024 version that lost 84 games despite returning a similar roster.</p><p>So the young, fun and welcoming, but also scrappy and resilient team character Venable has regularly praised his White Sox for carrying, is what he’s least certain of going forward.</p><p>“I don't think that we can make the assumption that that is going to exist next year,” Venable told the Sun-Times. “I'm hopeful, because it's going to be a lot of the same guys, but DNA changes.</p><p>“I saw it in Texas. Got this amazing group of guys, win a World Series, have success. Offseason maybe looks a little different, guys are in different situations in [salary arbitration], whatever, personal stuff happens. Next year, you're trying to create the magic and it’s hard to do.”</p><p>Venable spends a lot of time discussing the loose clubhouse atmosphere he works to facilitate, how he readily admits his mistakes because he wants his players to understand that mistakes are part of the game. But he would still concede the concept of team chemistry is better compared to alchemy. A silly, but concrete example: Mike Vasil won’t be the dugout wizard next year, he’ll be pitching.</p><p>“Each year is its own year with a bunch of different circumstances and things you can't control,” said bench coach Walker McKinven. “This is a special year. It's singular. It's on its own. We're trying to win, and go as deep as we can and get to the top.”</p><p>Part of the excitement, and also the grace, extended toward a 2026 White Sox team that’s been playing roughly .500 baseball since June 1, is that they’re ahead of schedule. The Sox arrive in Kansas City this week needing only to hold serve against two last-place teams to snag the last American League Wild Card spot, in a year where they were expected to finish in the Royals’ current position.</p><p>So it can only go up from here, and a young player group getting postseason experience is just a cherry on top…right?</p><p>“I suppose so, we’ve got a core group,” McKinven said, referring to the roster. “Them getting this experience and achieving what they’ve achieved this season is certainly building up a foundation that you want to grow off.”</p><p>“There is this transition as you get into September, as you get into meaningful baseball,” Venable said. “Where It does not matter what I do personally. It’s a mentality you have to go through. We have guys who are going through that for the first time, which is great.”</p><p>But are the Sox a top-10 MLB offense full of young hitters with upside, or the middle-of-the-pack unit they’ve been since the All-Star break? Are Noah Schultz and Hagen Smith ready to drive the future of the rotation, or are there 2-3 slots to fill over the offseason? Even without Vasil and Jordan Leasure, the Sox have only suffered an average level of injuries this year, and the bill for leading MLB in bullpen innings could come due next spring.</p><p>These are the areas of uncertainty that could make the Sox regret not pushing harder at the trade deadline. But after a year of hitting coaches coaxing out bat speed gains, improved defense, and Tristan Peters, Bryan Hudson and Randal Grichuk all being acquired and thriving after getting DFA’d by other smart organizations, roster problem-solving is the area for which Venable reserves the most confidence.</p><p>“What I am positive about is the progress of our [research and development] department, of our infrastructure, how we communicate things on both the pitching and the hitting side,” Venable said. “The underlying structural things that the organization is doing are going to expedite us being really good. Whatever our player group is and how they come together in the clubhouse is less predictable, but icing on the cake.”</p>

entries.title: Review: 'The Front Page' centers two things Chicagoans really love — great ensembles and local history
entries.summary: <p>Evanston’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/theater/2026/09/03/evanston-northlight-theater-chicago-suburbs-arts-annex" target="_blank" ><u>brand new Northlight Theatre</u></a> was swinging on Friday night with the inaugural production “The Front Page,” written in 1928. The atmosphere pre-show was electric, and I had more than one patron make a comment to me in the drink line about how the space feels even bigger when teeming with people.</p><p>I admit I had reservations about choosing such an old-timey story to launch an exciting theater venue that has pledged to focus on new plays. So it was a pleasant surprise when the high-energy farce about a group of 1930s newspaper writers paired perfectly with the excitement of the audience in the new space.</p><p>The show, originally written by Chicago newspaper writers Ben Hecht and Charles MacArthur, offers a critique of “jazz-journalism” — the cutthroat style of reporting ushered in by an era of widespread political corruption. It covers the mob’s influence on Chicago’s City Hall, and the response of journalists who leaned into covering scandals with tabloid-rich, salacious stories.</p><p>The real life people who influenced the production are intriguing in their own right. They include Terrible Tommy O’Connor, a man sentenced to death for killing a cop. He allegedly escaped the gallows with a gun smuggled into the jail in a pork sandwich. Then there’s William “Big Bill” Thompson, the former mayor of Chicago, who a panel of historians in 1933 dubbed the most corrupt mayor in American history. And you can’t forget Peter Hoffman, the former Cook County Sheriff in the pocket of Al Capone who was infamous for allowing mobsters to take unauthorized nights off from jail.</p><div from multiple publications operate out of a shared office inside Chicago’s Criminal Courts Building. Artistic director BJ Jones, who helmed this production, keeps the action humming even though both acts unfold in a single location. There is plenty of movement and at times it feels like a whirlwind of people in and out of doors, old ladies fainting, characters hiding in furniture, entrances and exits through windows. class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Michael Brosilow</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The show starts with a group of reporters playing poker, which is a nod to the true-to-life work culture of Hecht and MacArthur. Across the street, prisoner Earl Williams (John Drea, also seen in “Little Bear Ridge Road" at Steppenwolf and Broadway) is about to be hanged for murdering a cop. As the journalists are working the phones and preparing for the story — in these days, they didn’t actually write, but called the newsroom and verbally submitted the story — fellow reporter Hildy Johnson (Kate Fry) enters. She’s one of the best in business, but she announces her retirement, because she’s getting married and moving to Buffalo.</p><p>There are a few notable performances here, but Fry carries the show. Hildy is caught between two worlds: As a superstar reporter, she not only lands the big scoop, but she literally catches (and hides) the escaped killer. On the other hand, she’s ready for her next chapter, leaving the hustle bustle of the news biz to settle down with the stable accountant Brad Hefflefinger (Peter Moore).</p><p>Hildy is the central figure here, and Fry has a keen way of displaying her duality. In the newsroom, among the boys, she’s a tough-talking, sharp-witted pottymouth with talents that far exceed her peers. She often refers to herself, and is referred to by others, as a “newspaper man.” With Brad, she shows her soft side, and willingness to be a housewife, which her comrades enjoy poking fun at.</p><p>Underneath the hijinks, the play has a lot to say about political corruption and the need for people to speak truth to power. In one scene, Hildy’s editor, Walter Burns (Timothy Edward Kane, Fry’s actual husband), says, “The Chicago we love is being run by criminals and halfwits,” which earned a hearty groan from the audience.</p><p>Even with the stellar performance from Fry, I’m not completely sold by the script, adapted by Jeffrey Hatcher, nor am I convinced by Hildy’s ultimate decision to ditch the paper to “run the dishwasher.” The commentary on women in the workplace is there, and the story empowers Hildy to make her own choice while caught between two worlds, and two men (Walter and Brad), but it needed a touch more of a buildup for the ultimate payoff to fully satisfy.</p><p>Yet, this show works because it's fun. And it places an ensemble of well known, and highly talented, Chicago actors center stage in a production that centers something Chicagoans absolutely love: <i>Chicago</i>. This is a great way to welcome area audiences into one of the local theater community’s newest playhouses.<br></p>

entries.title: Settlement talks underway to revoke license of director at South Side funeral home where 56 bodies were found
entries.summary: <p>State regulators have held settlement negotiations to permanently revoke the license of the director of a South Deering funeral home where <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/01/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-clark-johanna-morgan" target="_blank" ><u>56 bodies were found rotting</u></a> in “deplorable conditions” last month, officials said Monday.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended Johanna Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer’s license Aug. 5 after investigators made the horrific discovery at South Chicago Chapel, owned by her husband, Clark Morgan, at 2939 E. 95th St.</p><p>During a brief teleconference hearing that marked the first step in adjudicating the grisly disciplinary case, attorneys for IDFPR and Johanna Morgan on Monday said they’ve discussed terms to potentially settle before advancing to a formal hearing scheduled later this fall.</p><p>Most state disciplinary cases are settled before reaching such a quasi-judicial hearing with witnesses and evidence — including past cases involving the Morgans, who had repeated run-ins with regulators in the decade leading up to the shocking discovery that has raised questions about Illinois’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice" target="_blank" ><u>disjointed oversight of the funeral industry</u></a>.</p><p>The Evergreen Park couple agreed to a consent order in June 2025 while facing disturbingly similar allegations at their now-shuttered crematory in Chicago Heights, where investigators from the Illinois Comptroller’s Office found 44 bodies piled up, along with hundreds of sets of mishandled cremated remains.</p><p>A patchwork state oversight system charges the comptroller’s office with regulating crematories while IDFPR licenses funeral directors and embalmers — leaving Illinois as one of four states that doesn’t conduct regular inspections of funeral home facilities.</p><p>The Morgans agreed to shut down Heights Crematory but admitted no wrongdoing under their 2025 agreement with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" target="_blank" ><u>the comptroller’s office</u></a>.</p><p>That case prompted IDFPR to visit the Morgans’ South Chicago Chapel in October 2025, when their investigators found “no serious concerns pertaining to the handling or storing of remains,” according to a timeline provided by Gov. JB Pritzker’s office.</p><p>But IDFPR still moved that month to revoke Johanna Morgan’s license, largely because her husband was transporting bodies under her purview with a forged license, according to agency records.</p><p>Clark Morgan had a state funeral director and embalmer intern license that he allowed to lapse in 2019, and which he then had revoked permanently in 2024 after picking up bodies at hospitals with a license showing “an altered expiration date,” authorities said.</p><p>The October 2025 case against Johanna Morgan was still pending when IDFPR officials visited South Chicago Chapel this summer, prompted by information that the chapel had utilized the crematory at Bohemian National Cemetery — which is facing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/bohemian-national-cemetery-under-investigation-for-improperly-stored-remains-equipment-failures" target="_blank" ><u>its own questions about improperly stored remains</u></a>.</p><p>That’s when investigators found dozens of bodies “in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions including rodent infestation, causing decomposition and maggot infestation of the bodies,” IDFPR officials said.</p><p>On Monday, an attorney for Johanna Morgan — who didn’t take part in the hearing — sought to consolidate the two disciplinary cases against her.</p><p>IDFPR Administrative Law Judge Donald Seasock rejected that motion “given the nature of the [2026] allegations, and the purpose of the act: protection of public health, safety and welfare.”</p><p>Attorneys for the Morgans have declined to comment. Seasock noted Johanna Morgan hasn’t formally answered the complaint against her as required by state rule, and he ordered a response within two weeks.</p><p>The couple got their respective licenses in the late 1990s and each faced their first suspensions in 2017 for failing to file state income taxes.</p><p>Johanna Morgan was reprimanded and fined $1,500 that year for transporting “a decedent across state lines for burial prior to obtaining required permits,” records show. She was also fined $5,000 in 2024 for failing to complete and file three death records “in a timely manner” in 2020.</p><p>The state has filed four tax liens on the couple’s south suburban home, outside of which Evergreen Park police found two bodies in a double-parked minivan during a bizarre June 2024 encounter.</p><p>Clark Morgan explained to officers that he had picked up the remains from a hospice center and had to stop to use the bathroom while en route to their crematory. Cook County prosecutors later advised police that the scenario violated no state law.</p><p>Illinois State Police have said they’re still conducting a criminal investigation in the Chicago Heights case, and assisting Chicago police in the ongoing South Chicago Chapel probe.</p><p>State lawmakers could try to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/18/south-deering-funeral-home-decomposing-bodies-illinois-lax-oversight-inspections" target="_blank" ><u>bolster funeral industry oversight</u></a> during the fall veto session in Springfield.</p><p><i>Contributing: Keenan Chen</i></p>

entries.title: Bears' Ben Johnson says QB Caleb Williams (hamstring) won't practice, but doesn't rule him out vs. Eagles
entries.summary: <p>Even with all <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ urgency and their confidence that they’re ready to push for a trip to the Super Bowl, they’d be wise to proceed cautiously with quarterback Caleb Williams’ hamstring injury.</p><p>It wasn’t clear Monday exactly what their plan was, but it’d be hard to imagine general manager Ryan Poles and coach Ben Johnson taking any chances by rushing him.</p><p>Johnson avoided boxing himself in with any sort of timetable or projection, saying only that he didn’t think Williams would practice this week leading up to the Bears’ home game Monday against the Eagles. He did not, however, rule out Williams for that game despite saying earlier in his weekly ESPN 1000 appearance that he would “likely miss some time.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/20/empathy-for-bears-qb-caleb-williams-aside-tyson-bagent-couldnt-ask-for-a-better-opportunity" >It’s almost certain that backup Tyson Bagent will work with the starters</a> when the Bears resume practice Wednesday, setting him up for his first start since 2023.</p><p>Johnson gave minimal information on Williams’ injury, perhaps out of gamesmanship or from annoyance with being peppered about it in the first 24 hours after Williams was carted to the locker room at the end of the Bears’ 9-3 loss to the Vikings.</p><p>When pressed for the next steps and whether Williams or the team would govern whether he was healthy enough to contribute, Johnson left it open-ended.</p><p>“He’s right now working through every avenue that he’s got available to get back on track here,” he said. “This guy’s a little bit different than the average human being. ... He gets back — he has in the past — a lot faster than what people can anticipate.</p><p>“He’s going to attack this with everything that he knows. He’s got a great team around him, both in this building and outside this building, and we’ll see where it goes from there.”</p><p>The Bears surely would prioritize the long term when it comes to Williams, of whom they’ve spoken openly about hoping to sign to a contract extension after the season. On that topic, all Johnson said was the team would make sure he’s “ready to go” before he returns.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/21/bears-qb-caleb-williams-hamstring-avoided-serious-hamstring-injury-mri" >Bears QB Caleb Williams has avoided serious hamstring injury</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/20/empathy-for-bears-qb-caleb-williams-aside-tyson-bagent-couldnt-ask-for-a-better-opportunity" >Empathy for Bears QB Caleb Williams aside, Tyson Bagent couldn’t ask for a better opportunity</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Women held up at gunpoint in 3 Lincoln Park attacks
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are looking for at least two men responsible for the armed robberies of three women, including two Sunday, prompting increased increased patrols in the Lincoln Park area.</p><p>The robbers, one of whom carried a gun, have confronted women who are alone on the street and demanded their jewelry, including rings, during the middle of the afternoon, occurring most recently Sunday in the 2200 block of North Halsted Street and in the 1800 block of West Larrabee Street between 3:30 and 3:45 p.m., according to a community alert issued by police. </p><p>On Thursday, another woman was attacked in the 300 block of West Webster Street about 2:15 p.m.</p><p>One of the robbers is described as being about 5-foot-10 with a heavyset build, wearing a gray ski mask, a black T-shirt and black pants. The other is shorter, about 5-foot-7, with a medium build wearing a black mask, a dark hooded sweatshirt and wielding a black gun, police said. </p><p>Chicago police confirmed that special attention has been placed in the area, including an increased patrol presence, 43rd Ward Ald. Timmy Knudsen said Monday.</p><p>Anyone with information should contact Area 3 detectives at 312-744-8236 or submit an anonymous tip, at CPDTIP.com, using reference No. P26-3-030.<br></p>

The wild-card round of the playoffs begins a week later, next Tuesday.</p>

entries.title: 3rd beluga whale dies after being moved to Shedd Aquarium from shuttered Marineland in Canada
entries.summary: <p>A beluga whale has died at the Shedd Aquarium after being transferred there from the shuttered Marineland aquarium in Ontario, Canada.</p><p>It was the third from Marineland to die at the Shedd, and the fourth from Marineland overall. </p><p>Osiris, a 26-year-old female beluga of "clinical concern," died Monday, the Shedd announced in a blog post. Her condition had been closely monitored since she arrived at the Shedd in late July, and she had periods of nutritional and social progress, the Shedd said. Osiris struggled to eat consistently, so it was difficult for her to get the nutrients and calories she needed.</p><p>"We also saw her commanding personality emerge and become more engaged with the other rescued whales," the Shedd said in the post. "Those were encouraging signs, but nutrition is only one measure of health, and in cases as complex as these, progress is rarely linear."</p><p>Osiris' behavior and respiratory patterns changed suddenly Monday morning and her condition declined rapidly, according to the aquarium. </p><p>Three other belugas from Marineland died in recent weeks. </p><p>At the Shedd, Peekachu, a 23-year-old female, died Aug. 25 and Rain, a 20-year-old female, died Sept. 2. Jelly Bean, another rescued beluga, died at Oceanogràfic Valencia in Spain last week. </p><p>Both aquariums are investigating each cause of death.</p><p>"When Shedd was asked to help with this rescue, we understood that these animals arrived with significant vulnerabilities and that the outcome for every individual could not be guaranteed," the Shedd said. "That uncertainty does not lessen the heartbreak of Osiris’s loss, or our responsibility to examine it with scientific rigor and open-hearted transparency."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/09/03/shedd-aquarium-beluga" >The Shedd also lost a third beluga recently</a> who was not from Marineland. Beethoven, a 34-year-old beluga already living at the Shedd, died Sept. 2.</p><p>Osiris, Rain, Jelly Bean and Peekachu were part of a group of 30 belugas evacuated after Marineland closed. The Niagara Falls aquarium had been under criticism for years over unsanitary conditions, and animal rights activists have questioned whether transferring the belugas is safe. Many whales at Marineland were likely sick and air travel could make their illnesses worse, they said.</p><p>"The deaths of Peekachu and Rain bring up very serious questions about their health status prior to being transferred to Shedd and the judgement used in that decision,” Lori Marino, co-founder and president of the planned Whale Sanctuary Project in Port Hilford Bay, Nova Scotia, told the Sun-Times after the deaths of the first two belugas who came to the Shedd from Marineland.</p><p>Marineland closed due to major financial issues and threatened to euthanize the belugas if they couldn't be moved to a new home.</p>

entries.title: Preservationists seek landmark status for Englewood mansion built by Mrs. O'Leary's son
entries.summary: <p>An endangered Englewood mansion built by the Victorian era man-about-town and gambler James "Big Jim" O'Leary — his mother and her cow were blamed for starting the Great Chicago Fire — should be granted preliminary landmark status, the city's two leading preservation groups said Monday.</p><p>Landmarks Illinois and Preservation Chicago told the Commission on Chicago Landmarks' Program Committee that the designation is needed to protect the vacant 125-year-old O'Leary Mansion, 726 W. Garfield Blvd., from demolition.</p><p>The 33-room house is currently in demolition court under a raft of code violations. Inspectors reported the home's condition as "dangerous."</p><p>"We're looking at a number of factors [as reasons to landmark the house], from the architecture to the architect, to the people connected with this place," Landmarks Illinois Interim President and CEO Frank Butterfield said before the meeting.</p><p>Built in 1901, according to building permits Butterfield unearthed, the three-story mansion was designed by Zachary Taylor Davis, an architect whose works include Wrigley Field and the old — and dearly missed — Comiskey Park.</p><p>The red sandstone-fronted house is a Renaissance Revival riot, with details that include turrets, an ornate circular attic window and two-story bay windows flanking a prominent four-columned front porch.</p><p>O'Leary's initials can be found in the facade's terra cotta detail.</p><p>The home is one of many surviving examples of the high-style homes and apartment buildings that were constructed along Garfield Boulevard from Wells Street to Western Avenue for the well-to-do between the late 19th and early 20th centuries.</p><p>Among the boulevard's plump-pocketed set was James O'Leary, one of Patrick and Catherine O'Leary's five children.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9f0000" name="image-9f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" alt="Weeds mingle with the architectural details surrounding an attic window of the O'Leary Mansion at 726 W. Garfield Blvd." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/06d8a5d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7945x4459+0+420/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9d%2F7d%2F4bc823194b218f16e01933926094%2Foleary-2609220052.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a745322/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7945x4459+0+420/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9d%2F7d%2F4bc823194b218f16e01933926094%2Foleary-2609220052.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/06d8a5d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7945x4459+0+420/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9d%2F7d%2F4bc823194b218f16e01933926094%2Foleary-2609220052.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Weeds mingle with the architectural details surrounding an attic window of the O’Leary Mansion at 726 W. Garfield Blvd.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Catherine O'Leary became part of Chicago folklore when she was accused of starting the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. According to the since-debunked story, she was milking a cow in the family's DeKoven Street barn when the animal kicked over a lantern and touched off the historic conflagration.</p><p>James O'Leary, who was two years old at the time, grew up to become wealthy. He owned a gambling house and saloon at 41st and Halsted streets that — as fate would have it — burned down in the massive Union Stock Yards fire of 1910.</p><p>"He was a gambling boss in the Union Stock Yards neighborhood and was said to be willing to gamble on anything from sports to elections to even the weather," Butterfield said. </p><p>"So he made quite a living for himself, and as such, was able to commission quite a prominent building," he said of O'Leary's Garfield Boulevard manse.</p><p>O'Leary died in the house in 1925 at age 56. His mother died in 1895.</p><p>Landmarks Illinois and Preservation Chicago decided to speak up for the house because both organizations "have heard from constituents in the neighborhood, from local residents, and this is a priority for both of our organizations," Butterfield said.</p><p>"So, when we have opportunities to work together, we are more powerful with a joint mission than we would be for one individually," he said.</p><p>The home's owner was absent from the committee meeting. And who owns the 6,200-square-foot house is murky. It was last listed for sale in 2024 at $450,000, listing details on Redfin show.</p><p>"We hope to have a good steward come forward to adopt the building and restore it and consent to landmark designation," Preservation Chicago Executive Director Ward Miller said.</p><p>The Program Committee forwarded the O'Leary mansion and other landmark recommendations from the public to the Department of Planning and Development’s Historic Preservation Division for possible follow-up.</p><p>The division could take a pass on the recommendation, or after researching the building, the staffers could prepare a report that asks the full landmarks commission to grant the house a preliminary designation.</p><p>The latter is the better move and would protect the historic and architecturally significant building from demolition and wonky, non-historic alterations.</p><p>"It's really important that we protect this building," Miller said. "And we will be not only supporting it before the program committee ... but also in court in the coming weeks."</p>
