entries.title: Pritzker's net worth jumps by $1 billion since becoming Illinois governor in 2019
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker’s net worth has jumped by $1 billion since first taking office and now stands at $4.2 billion overall, but his vast fortune pales compared to the state’s wealthiest individual, a new report by Forbes Magazine shows.</p><p>The two-term Democrat and potential 2028 presidential candidate was among nearly 30 Illinoisans to land on Forbes’ 2026 World Billionaires list, a coveted status symbol for those rare wealthy few whose bank accounts number 10 digits and longer.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/09/21/illinois-governor-jb-pritzker-interview-glp-1-diabetes-weight-loss" >Pritzker,</a> an heir to the Hyatt Hotel empire, has been on that list since 2010. And even though he had a major jump in his net worth over the last year, he dropped in the overall rankings of the richest people in the world.</p><p>According to Forbes’ list, Pritzker ranks 1,108th in wealth globally. His current estimated net worth of $4.2 billion is about $500 million more than he was worth last year and $1 billion dollars more than he was worth at the start of his governorship in 2019.</p><p>Despite the increase in his wealth, Pritzker saw a slight drop in Forbes’ ranking. Last year, Pritzker ranked 979th richest in the world.</p><p>The governor’s office did not respond to a WBEZ request for comment from Pritzker about his placement on Forbes’ list.</p><p>The governor is among at least 28 Illinoisans on the Forbes list, but he isn’t close to being the state’s richest resident.</p><p>That place is held by Lukas Walton, the grandson of Walmart founder Sam Walton and part-owner of the retailing behemoth he inherited following his father’s death in 2005.</p><p>Walton, of Chicago, is worth an estimated $44.4 billion and saw the value of his overall financial portfolio increase by a whopping $6.5 billion from 2025, Forbes reported.</p><p>His wealth ranks 40th overall globally.</p><p>The second-richest person in Illinois is Charlie Mills, chairman of Medline, which is a private distributor of medical supplies in the U.S. Mills’ father and uncle started the company in 1966.</p><p>Mills, who is from Winnetka and ranked 279th globally, appeared on the Forbes list for the first time this year and is estimated to be worth $10.6 billion.</p><p>Ranking No. 3 among Illinois’ financial elite is real estate tycoon and gambling magnate Neil Bluhm. He owns marquee Chicago properties like 900 North Michigan and the Ritz-Carlton Chicago, and has a financial stake in the Rivers Casino in Des Plaines. Bluhm’s rank on the Forbes’ global list of billionaires is 422nd.</p><p>Bluhm, of Chicago, has an estimated net worth of about $9.4 billion, jumping about $2 billion from last year, the magazine reported.</p><p>Founder and Executive Chairman Patrick Ryan of Chicago-based Ryan Specialty Holdings, a wholesale brokerage and specialty insurance firm, is the fourth-richest person from Illinois.</p><p>Ryan ranks 461st with an estimated net worth of $9.15 billion. He saw a drop of nearly $4 billion from last year. Forbes also lists his residence as Winnetka.</p><p>Following Ryan is Ty Warner at 557th place, the creator of Beanie Babies and a resident of Oak Brook.</p><p>Warner sold Beanie Babies and invested in a high-end hotel portfolio that includes the Four Seasons in New York and a resort in Mexico. Warner has an estimated $8.6 billion net worth, marking a nearly $2 million increase from last year.</p><p>Each of the top five richest individuals from Illinois made both Forbes’ World’s Billionaires list and the 400 Richest Americans list.</p><p>This year, for the first time since 2010, Pritzker did not make the Forbes 400 list. The lowest net worth on that list this year came in at $4.4 billion, and Pritzker was about $200 million short.</p><p>The world billionaires list also included Uline owners Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein and other members of the Pritzker and Mills families.</p><p>Also included is Los Angeles Dodgers owner Mark Walter, CEO of investment firm Guggenheim Partners. He ranks in 528th place with an estimated $7.3 billion net worth. His portfolio jumped more than $1 billion since last year. Walter lives in Chicago.</p><p>Another Chicago baseball tycoon made the list: White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >Justin Ishbia.</a></p><p>Ishbia, who could take control of the potentially playoffs-bound South Side baseball team as early as 2029, has a net worth of $6.36 billion. That’s up from $5.1 billion last year, Forbes reported.</p>

entries.title: Cleanup begins in Douglass Park after rain-soaked Riot Fest left it a mud pit
entries.summary: <p>It’s a wrap on Riot Fest 2026. But one big reminder of the weekend still lingers in Douglass Park — all the mud after heavy rains over the weekend turned the grounds into a shell of itself by the end of the final set.</p><p>One Little Village community group, Únete La Villita, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/Ddjo1-txkDV/" target="_blank" ><u>posted on Instagram</u></a> Monday that the park is “completely destroyed,” adding concerns about the “long-term effects of the fest that’s ‘just three days’” and adding they will be documenting the restoration over the next year.</p><p>Riot Fest Founder Mike Petryshyn said in a statement Monday afternoon that his team’s “responsibility does not end when the festival does. We are committed to restoring the park, working alongside the Park District and the community, and seeing that work through.” In addition to tackling the immediate repairs, that also includes working with the 24th Ward and the Chicago Park District to work on "other underlying conditions within Douglass Park" such as drainage and plumbing for "longer-term improvements," according to Riot Fest's statement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-270000" name="image-270000"></a> <picture the stage. As fans were leaving for the final time, some lost their shoes to the sludge, while others got stuck in it and were helped by strangers in a communal effort to work through it.</p><p>After getting through the weekend, a large part of the focus now is on what repairs will look like for Douglass Park in the days to come.</p><p>Beyond the actual three days the event is held in the park, Riot Fest organizers are given time to build and break down the site. On the <a class="Link" href="https://riotfest.org/park-impact/#access" target="_blank" ><u>Riot Fest website,</u></a> the 2026 timeline lists Sept. 21-24 as the designated production load-out, cleaning and restoration window while Sept. 25 was listed as the date the park would be fully open to the public, though completion of load-out has since been pushed to Sept. 29, "weather and ground conditions permitting," according to the festival. “Immediately following load-out, Riot Fest, its restoration team, and the Chicago Park District will assess the affected areas and begin implementing the restoration plan,” organizers said in a statement.</p><p>As of press time, the office of Ald. Monique Scott (24th) did not respond to comment about the projected timeline, what repairs will include and an estimate of the total cost.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f50000" name="image-f50000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3f6da45/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6860x3850+0+363/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7f%2F6c%2Fbb3bf2f94137baa388bfa62c2537%2Friotfestday3photos-260921-83.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1eca3fb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6860x3850+0+363/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7f%2F6c%2Fbb3bf2f94137baa388bfa62c2537%2Friotfestday3photos-260921-83.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0fca28b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6860x3850+0+363/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7f%2F6c%2Fbb3bf2f94137baa388bfa62c2537%2Friotfestday3photos-260921-83.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Attendees push a stroller through deep mud as it rains in Douglass Park on Day 3 of Riot Fest, Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0fca28b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6860x3850+0+363/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7f%2F6c%2Fbb3bf2f94137baa388bfa62c2537%2Friotfestday3photos-260921-83.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/924670e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6860x3850+0+363/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7f%2F6c%2Fbb3bf2f94137baa388bfa62c2537%2Friotfestday3photos-260921-83.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0fca28b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6860x3850+0+363/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7f%2F6c%2Fbb3bf2f94137baa388bfa62c2537%2Friotfestday3photos-260921-83.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Attendees push a stroller through deep mud as it rains in Douglass Park on Day 3 of Riot Fest.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Fans had mixed feelings about the mess. “As long as you’re counting one foot in front of the other, you’ll be OK. … It’s punk rock, it’s Riot Fest. Everyone is having a good time,” said Alex Ramos of Rogers Park, a repeat attendee who came out Sunday for Pierce the Veil and Pennywise. “We’ve still been seeing everybody but just battling the elements, as you can imagine.”</p><p> Joe Theis, 52, who traveled from Denver, agreed that attendees seemed to be taking the mud in stride. “I never made it to Woodstock ‘99 with the mud people and everything, but this is as close as I've ever been,” he said. “Everybody seems to be managing it OK.” </p><p>Grace Elliott, 35, of Cleveland, Ohio, uses a walker and described difficulties navigating the park as conditions worsened. “The wheels of my rollator were getting gummed up with mud and grass, and even going over the wood chips, it was more like dragging my mobility aid through and … my feet were stuck in the ground.”</p><p> Elliott visited an onsite accessibility tent and called the crew there “very empathetic,” though she felt out of options and eventually decided to leave.</p><p>“They didn't straight up tell us you have to go home, but there weren't really options for many people, especially people like me who use a mobility aid,” she added, suggesting future accommodations like more metal ramps and pathways and utilizing golf carts or ATVs to help those with limited mobility get around the park during inclement weather. </p><p>Riot Fest’s current <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/entertainment-and-culture/2025/04/10/3-year-riot-fest-deal-draws-mixed-reviews-from-residents-around-douglass-park" target="_blank" ><u>three-year contract</u></a> in Douglass Park runs through 2027. Lauren Quinn, the Chicago Park District’s deputy director of revenue, said the department will generate roughly $3 million to $4.5 million from the deal via annual permit fees.</p><p>In 2026, the deal requires Riot Fest organizers to pay $5.375 per ticket. For 2027, it increases to $5.50 per ticket, estimated at 150,000 tickets sold for all three days.</p><p>From the money raised, the park district has a 30% “give back” policy in place specifically for Douglass Park, meaning $900,000 to $1.2 million is allocated solely for improvements to the North Lawndale grounds. The contract also stipulates that Riot Fest will give an additional 10% give back “to capital improvements in Douglass Park.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b10000" name="image-b10000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/31ce10c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5341x2998+0+280/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff6%2F99%2F0d14747c4b3f84212165fd5806ee%2Friotmudreact-260922-16.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/302acd9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5341x2998+0+280/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff6%2F99%2F0d14747c4b3f84212165fd5806ee%2Friotmudreact-260922-16.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/789f655/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5341x2998+0+280/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff6%2F99%2F0d14747c4b3f84212165fd5806ee%2Friotmudreact-260922-16.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Douglass Park after Riot Fest weekend in North Lawndale, Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. The event permittee will also have to pay any costs to restore "identified damaged areas."</p><p>Event organizers stated that "immediately following load-out, Riot Fest, its restoration team, and the Chicago Park District will assess the affected areas and begin implementing the restoration plan." They have noted that the repairs are "expected to include soil preparation, aeration, seeding, grading, and sod replacement where appropriate" and may require nearly three acres of sod.</p><p>It's similar to Lollapalooza negotiations between the Chicago Park District and organizer C3 Presents who also pay annually to re-beautify Grant Park. entries.title: Bears' Ben Johnson has problems to fix that have nothing to do with the QB
entries.summary: <p>The worst loss of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a>’s Bears tenure was unquestionably the second game of last season, when he returned to Ford Field and left with a 52-21 defeat.</p><p></p><p>The second-worst might have been the second game of this season — and that was before Bears quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/21/bears-ben-johnson-says-qb-caleb-williams-hamstring-wont-practice-but-doesnt-rule-him-out-vs-eagles" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> pulled his hamstring midway through the fourth quarter of a sloppy, soggy 9-3 loss to the Vikings.</p><p></p><p>After talking openly about wanting to score the most points in NFL history, and then posting 59 in the opener, Johnson engineered an offense that scored three.</p><p></p><p>The much-ballyhooed chess match between Johnson and Brian Flores went to the Vikings’ defensive coordinator, who used an extreme blitz rate to keep the coach and quarterback on their heels. After averaging 27.5 points in his career against Flores, Johnson managed just three.</p><p></p><p>In a rainstorm, Flores blitzed Williams on 27 of his 33 dropbacks. That 82% rate would have been the third-highest in any game since 2018, per NFL Next Gen Stats. The Vikings shifted to the Bears' right, too, trying to take away their most successful direction on run plays.</p><p></p><p>Williams won’t practice this week. While Johnson refused to rule him out for Monday night, it seems likely that backup Tyson Bagent will face the Eagles.</p><p></p><p>The most alarming part of Sunday’s result, though, was the fact that Johnson needs to fix problems that go far beyond who’s playing quarterback.</p><p>The Bears were brutal in the red zone, bad on their field goal attempts and needed to regroup at halftime for their run game to improve. The penalties they committed, though, gnawed most at Johnson on Monday afternoon.</p><p></p><p>“The penalties were a major factor, more so than the weather or anything other …” he said. “It was the penalties and things that we really hadn’t seen in practice. They showed up there on game day.”</p><p>In the second quarter, the Bears committed three-straight penalties on offense — an illegal shift, holding and intentional grounding — and then, after one clean play, a false start on, of all people, center Garrett Bradbury.</p><p></p><p>“We always ask ourselves, ‘Was it us or them?’” guard Jonah Jackson said. “And it was an 'us' situation.”</p><p>That’s not as reassuring as it sounds.</p><p>They didn’t commit an offensive penalty in the second half, but by then the damage was done.</p><p>The Bears have a penalty problem. Sunday’s games, they are tied for the third-most flags in the NFL, with 20. Only the Panthers and the Chargers have been flagged more on offense than the Bears’ 12.</p><p></p><p>“Even when we felt like we were getting a little momentum and staying ahead of the schedule there, we kind of shot ourselves in the foot a couple times,” Johnson said.</p><p>They found other ways to do it, too.</p><p>In the first half, the Bears’ two running backs — D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai — ran 12 times for just 27 yards. The Bears marched down to the 1-yard line on the first drive of the third quarter, only for Swift to fumble on first-and-goal.</p><p>Williams likely would have run for a touchdown from the 6 on the play in which he crumpled to the ground. Johnson was frustrated by the Bears’ inability to score on three Bagent throws from the Vikings’ 12 in the game’s final seconds. On the first, Bagent threw incomplete to Luther Burden along the left sideline. On the second, he threw incomplete at the feet of tight end Colston Loveland at the goal line. And on the third, he was sacked by Dallas Turner after the clock expired.</p><p></p><p>“You start with a first-and-goal from the 1, a first-and-goal from the 6 and … three shots at the end of the game — and we end up getting zero points out of all three of those opportunities,” Johnson said. “That’s really the tale of the second half.”</p><p></p><p>The Bears reached the 5-yard line and twice and didn’t score either time. They didn't score at all in the red zone. Despite their 59-point outburst in Week 1, the Bears rank 19<sup>th</sup> in red zone percentage through Sunday.</p><p></p><p>That needs fixing. So does the field goal operation.</p><p>Playing his second game, Beau Gardner snapped the ball high on the Bears’ first attempt, a 50-yard Cairo Santos field goal. The second snap was high, too, and blocked by Isaiah Rodgers with the Bears trailing by three with about six minutes to play. Gardner might have snapped it too soon, too, as both wing blockers seemed to be flat-footed. Before Sunday, the Bears only had two field goals under 23 yards blocked since 2000.</p><p>“That first field goal was a warning shot as far as I’m concerned,” Johnson said. “No. 2 was right off the edge. If [Rodgers] didn’t touch it, then he was darn close to touching it then. Something we addressed on the sideline and we weren’t able to get corrected the second time. So [we’re] certainly in a race to get that right.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/21/bears-ben-johnson-says-qb-caleb-williams-hamstring-wont-practice-but-doesnt-rule-him-out-vs-eagles" >Bears’ Ben Johnson says QB Caleb Williams (hamstring) won’t practice, but doesn’t rule him out vs. Eagles</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Evanston man, a U.S. citizen, injured in Sunday confrontation with federal immigration agents
entries.summary: <p>Police in north suburban Evanston are investigating an incident involving a resident who is a U.S. citizen and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents Sunday morning.</p><p>The incident happened near Howard Street and Dodge Avenue around 9:49 a.m. Officers were dispatched after an unknown caller reported hearing two men arguing and someone stating that an individual would be taken into custody.</p><p>When Evanston officers arrived, they found an adult male on the ground with several people assisting him. A <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/reel/1805994363913682" target="_blank" ><u>video</u></a> posted to Facebook shows the man on the ground with two agents trying to take him into custody despite his pleas that he’s a U.S. citizen.</p><p>The man can be heard shouting at the agents as a passerby records the incident.</p><p>The more than 3-minute video shows two agents letting go of the man and leaving the scene in separate vehicles, with the subject still on the ground.</p><p>The man told officers his neck, head and teeth were injured.</p><p>The federal agents told Evanston police they attempted to identify an individual resembled a person they were seeking. The agent told police the individual refused to provide identification, was detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention.</p><p>Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned he was a U.S. citizen. He was released.</p><p>The agent also said the federal agents left the area after protesters began to gather because they feared they would be attacked.</p><p>Officers later contacted the detained individual, an adult Evanston resident, at a local hospital.</p><p>"This is something that that shouldn't be happening in my city. It shouldn't be happening on the streets of Evanston, but it shouldn't be happening in any city across the country," said Nathan Ryan with Sanctuary Evanston, a rapid-response group based in the north suburb. </p><p>Sanctuary Evanston and the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights released a joint statement condemning the violence and calling on elected officials to investigate the incident.</p><p>“Federal agents assaulting people in the streets does not make our community safer for anyone. Regardless of status, every single one of our neighbors is worthy of dignity and safety,” the two groups said.</p><p>U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could not immediately be reached for comment. Evanston police continue to investigate the incident, which comes at a time of heightened interaction with federal immigration agents. </p><p>In Austin, Texas on Sunday, an ICE officer shot and wounded a man during a traffic stop and anti-ICE protesters gathered near the scene for hours afterward, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/austin-texas-ice-shooting-driver-wilber-perez-ebdb9d481d28e322f62c15f1076f3c18" target="_blank" >according to the Associated Press</a>.</p><p>Austin's police chief said the man who was shot was in serious but stable condition at a hospital Sunday afternoon. An immigration attorney identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man. Garcas Perez was making a DoorDash delivery before being shot .</p><p>DHS said the man is in custody pending removal from the country, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>Closer to home, <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/09/20/federal-agents-pepper-spray-10-protesters-outside-broadview-ice-center-on-1-year-anniversary-of-start-of-violent-clashes/" target="_blank" >federal officers used pepper spray against protesters</a> outside the Broadview ICE facility on Saturday as demonstrators blocked a driveway into the facility, according to Block Club Chicago.</p><p>"This isn't about immigration enforcement. That this is about violence," Ryan said. "The only thing I think that is like more horrifying than seeing federal agents beating people up on the street is seeing federal agents beat people up on the street without repercussions and accountability."</p><p><i>Michael Puente is a reporter and anchor with WBEZ. Reach him at mpuente@wbez.org.</i> <br></p>
